abat-jour.etymology: Compound formed in seventeenth-century French from abattre ('to beat or cast down', 3rd-person stem abat-) and jour ('daylight'). Before naming a lampshade, an abat-jour was a slanted cellar skylight angled to throw daylight downward into a basement.

history.meaning: reflector or shade casting lamp light downward

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: abat-jour (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: abat-jour

abat-jour.notes: Because **jour** sits inside the verb-object phrase *abattre le jour*, traditional grammar treats **des abat-jour** as invariable in the plural.

abeille.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Old Occitan abelha ('bee'), itself inherited from Classical Latin apicula ('little bee', diminutive of apis), replacing northern Old French ef / é after sound wear reduced apis to a single vowel.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: abeille (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: abeille

abeille.notes: Because Latin **apis** eroded in northern French to a tiny monosyllable (**ef**, plural **és**), speakers adopted southern **abeille** so the word for 'bee' stayed clear and unmistakable.

abri.etymology: Abri derives as a back-formation from Old French abrier ('to cover, shelter from the cold', from Late Latin apricare 'to warm in the sun').
abri.notes: **À l'abri de la pluie** = sheltered from the rain.

accompagner.etymology: Inherited from Old French acompaignier ('to take as a companion, go along with'), formed on compain / compagnon from Late Latin companionem (cum 'with' + panis 'bread' — literally 'one with whom you share bread').

history.meaning: to go with; to accompany musically

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: accompagner (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: accompagner

accompagner.notes: In both table fellowship and chamber music, **accompagner** preserves the warm image of sharing bread (**pain**) at the same table.

accord.etymology: Accord is a noun formed from accorder, to bring into agreement. The Académie records the twelfth-century spelling acort.

acier.etymology: Inherited via Old French acier from Late Latin aciarium ('hardened edge-iron, steel'), derived from Classical Latin acies ('sharp cutting edge, blade point'), because steel was first forged specifically to give iron tools and weapons a durable edge.

history.meaning: hardened iron for cutting edges, steel

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: acier (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: acier

acier.notes: From the same Indo-European sharpness root come French **aigu** ('sharp, high-pitched') and **aigre** ('sour').

agence.etymology: A seventeenth-century French derivative of agent. The word developed the modern senses of an intermediary business, an official organisation, and the offices where such work takes place.
agence.notes:
- Common collocations: **agence de voyages**, **agence immobilière**, **agence de presse**.
- The word is feminine: **une agence**.

ah.etymology: This interjection continues an expressive cry rather than an ordinary noun. The Académie records eleventh-century A or Ha and notes the same exclamation in Latin.

aide.etymology: The noun was formed from the older French verb behind aider. Ninth-century aiudha meant the act of helping; the shorter form aïe is recorded in the twelfth century.

aider.etymology: Aider comes from Latin adjutare, a repeated-action form related to adjuvare, to help. The French verb is recorded from the tenth century.

aiguille.etymology: Inherited via Old French aguille from Late Latin acucula ('small needle, pin'), diminutive of Classical Latin acus ('needle'), from the root of acutus ('sharp, pointed').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: aiguille (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: aiguille

aiguille.notes: Notice the pronunciation **/eɡɥij/** (where *-gu-* before *-i-* sounds like */ɡɥi/*, unlike **guide** */ɡid/*), and how French uses **les aiguilles** for the hands of a clock.

aller.etymology: The Académie traces aller to Latin ambulare, to walk or move about. The proposed route through a shortened military command is uncertain. Other Latin verbs survive within its conjugation: ire in the future and conditional, and vadere in several present forms and the singular imperative.
aller.notes: Aller forms the near future: je vais manger. Allez ! and Allons ! can also encourage someone, roughly come on.

allié.etymology: Allié began as the past participle of allier, to join or ally. The Académie records fourteenth-century alliet; the participle also became a noun for an ally.

allô.etymology: Allô is a nineteenth-century borrowing of American English hallo or hello. The early French spelling hallo preserves the link with that greeting.

alors.etymology: Alors joins à and the older adverb lors. It is recorded from the twelfth century, although the Académie notes that it remained uncommon until the fifteenth.

amande.etymology: Inherited via Old French almande / amande from Vulgar Latin amandula, an everyday alteration of Classical Latin amygdala, borrowed from Ancient Greek amygdálē ('almond').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: amande (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: amande

amande.notes: Learned anatomical French re-borrowed the Greek-Latin form directly as **amygdale** ('tonsil, amygdala', named for its almond shape).

ami.etymology: Ami continues Latin amicus, used both as an adjective and a noun. The eleventh-century French form amic still shows the older final consonant.

an.etymology: An descends from Latin annus, year. The Académie dates the French noun to the eleventh century.

anniversaire.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical and Medieval Latin anniversarius ('returning every year'), compound of annus ('year') + versus ('turned', past participle of vertere).

history.meaning: day that comes round each year

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: anniversaire (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: anniversaire

anniversaire.notes: In everyday French, **un anniversaire** means both 'birthday' (**Joyeux anniversaire!**) and 'anniversary' (**anniversaire de mariage**).

anse.etymology: Inherited from Latin ansa ('handle of a jug or cup, loop, grip'), which survived directly into Old French anse for the curved ear-like handle of a vessel or basket.

history.meaning: loop handle of a vessel, grip
curved handle of a pot, cup, or basket

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: anse (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: anse

anse.notes: French divides English 'handle' by shape: **une anse** is a curved loop (teacup, basket), **une poignée** is a grip/door handle, and **un manche** is a straight shaft (pan, broom, knife).

appel.etymology: Appel is a noun formed from appeler, to call. It is recorded from the eleventh century; its modern telephone sense extends the older idea of a call.

appeler.etymology: Appeler comes from Latin appellare, whose senses included approaching someone and addressing them. The French verb is recorded from the tenth century.

apprenti.etymology: Inherited from Old French aprentiz ('learner bound to a craft master'), formed with suffix -iz (< Latin -icius) on the stem of aprendre ('to learn'), from Latin apprehendere ('to take hold of, grasp with the mind').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: apprenti (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: apprenti

apprenti.notes: Old plural **apprentis** dropped the internal *-t-* before *-s*, and singular **apprenti** was later reshaped from the spoken plural.

aquarelle.etymology: Borrowed in the late 18th century from Italian acquerello / acquarella ('thin water-based pigment wash'), derived from acqua ('water') < Classical Latin aqua.

cognates.meaning: from French aquarelle and Latin aqua
native inherited doublet of Latin aqua

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: aquarelle (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: aquarelle

aquarelle.notes: **Aquarelle** (borrowed via Italian) and **eau** (inherited directly) both go back to the exact same four-letter Latin noun **aqua**.

argile.etymology: From Latin argilla ('white potter's clay'), borrowed from Ancient Greek árgillos, built on argós ('shining, white') after the pale colour of fine kaolin and potter's earth.

rootFamily.gloss: silver; money (from the same Indo-European 'white/shining' root)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: argile (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: argile

arriver.etymology: Arriver comes from Vulgar Latin *arripare (ad + ripa 'riverbank, shore'): originally a maritime and river word meaning 'to reach the bank, come ashore', before generalising to 'to arrive, happen'!
arriver.notes: Takes **être** in the passé composé (*elle est arrivée*). **J'arrive!** = Coming! / On my way!

assiette.etymology: Inherited from Old French assiete ('act of seating guests at table; the dish set at each diner's place'), feminine participial noun from asseoir ('to seat, set down') < Vulgar Latin assedere.

history.meaning: to sit beside, set in place
seating arrangement; course set before a guest

cognates.meaning: from Anglo-Norman asetz / assiette in legal accounting

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: assiette (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: assiette

assiette.notes: The older sense 'way of sitting steady' survives in the idiom **ne pas être dans son assiette** ('to feel out of sorts').

assistant.etymology: Assistant is the present participle of assister used as a noun. The Académie dates this development to the fourteenth century.

attendre.etymology: Attendre comes from Latin attendere, to direct one’s attention towards something. The eleventh-century French spelling was atendre; waiting and expecting developed around that idea of attention.

au.etymology: Au is the contraction of the preposition à and the masculine article le. It is a grammatical combination, not the unrelated chemical symbol Au. The Académie describes its use under à.

aube.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin alba ('dawn'), substantivized feminine of Classical Latin albus ('dull white'), elliptical for alba lux ('the white light on the horizon before sunrise').

history.meaning: first white light of morning, daybreak

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: aube (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: aube

aube.notes: Latin *al-* vocalized regularly to *au-* before consonants in Old French (*alba* -> **aube**, *alterum* -> **autre**, *calidum* -> **chaud**).

aussi.etymology: Aussi developed from an older combination of al, meaning something else, and si, meaning thus. The Académie records twelfth-century alsi in a comparison expression; the modern adverb also acquired the sense too.

automne.etymology: Borrowed in Old French from Classical Latin autumnus ('autumn, harvest season'), a word of ancient Italic or Etruscan origin already opaque to Roman grammarians. The Latin -mn- spelling was restored in Middle French even though only /n/ is pronounced.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: automne (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: automne

automne.notes: The **-m-** is silent in **automne** (/otɔn/), resurging aloud in the adjective **automnal** (/otɔmnal/).

autre.etymology: Autre descends from Latin alter, the other of two. Tenth-century French distinguished masculine altre and feminine altra.

aux.etymology: Aux combines the preposition à with the plural article les. Like singular au, it belongs to the history of French preposition–article contractions rather than being an independent borrowed noun.

avaler.etymology: Avaler is derived from aval, downwards or downstream. Its eleventh-century intransitive sense was to descend; the swallowing sense developed as making something go down the throat.

avance.etymology: Avance is a noun built from avancer ('to move forward', from Vulgar Latin *abantiare, built on ab + ante 'from before').
avance.notes: **Être en avance** = to be early (ahead of schedule); **à l'avance** = beforehand.

avec.etymology: Avec continues a reconstructed Popular Latin combination *apu(d)-hoc, approximately with this, strengthening apud, near or with. The early French forms avuec, avoc and avoec are recorded in the eleventh century.

averse.etymology: Formed in early modern French by fusing the adverbial phrase à verse ('pouring down in buckets', as in il pleut à verse), built on verser ('to pour, tip over') from Latin versare.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: averse (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: averse

averse.notes: Compare **renverser** ('to spill or knock over') and **verser** ('to pour tea or soup'), both from the same root.

avoir.etymology: Avoir descends from Latin habere. The Académie dates the French verb to the ninth century. Its central meaning concerns possession, and it also serves as an auxiliary in compound tenses.
avoir.notes:
- *Avoir* is used for age and many states: *avoir chaud, froid, faim, soif, peur, raison, tort*.
- *Il y a* means 'there is/are' and also 'ago': *il y a deux ans*.
- Along with *être*, it is one of the two auxiliary verbs of French.

bail.etymology: Deverbal noun from Old French baillier ('to hand over, entrust, administer'), inherited from Classical Latin bajulare ('to carry a burden, take charge of'), from bajulus ('porter, carrier').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French bail / baillif

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: bail (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: bail

bail.notes: Plural **baux** preserves the historical vocalization of *-l* before *-s* (**un bail**, **des baux**), and colloquially **ça fait un bail!** means 'it has been ages!'.

balcon.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian balcone ('projecting gallery or window platform'), itself derived from Lombardic *balko ('wooden beam, timber platform').

cognates.meaning: balcony via Italian; balk ('beam') from Old English balca

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: balcon (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: balcon

balcon.notes: Renaissance Italian architecture brought **le balcon** into French cities, where wrought-iron railings later became a hallmark of classic facades.

banc.etymology: Inherited from Old French banc ('long wooden seat; market counter'), borrowed early from Frankish *bank ('bench, shelf').

cognates.meaning: bench is the native Germanic cousin; bank came via Italian banca
italianate relatives from the same Germanic root

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: banc (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)

banc.notes: The final *-c* in **un banc** **/bɑ̃/** is completely silent (just like **blanc** **/blɑ̃/** and **franc** **/fʁɑ̃/**).

bassin.etymology: Inherited from Old French bacin ('wide bowl, water basin'), from Late/Medieval Latin baccinum ('water vessel'), widely traced to a Gaulish root *bacca ('trough, bowl').

history.meaning: fountain basin, garden pool, river basin

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: bassin (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: bassin

bassin.notes: In public French parks and squares, **le bassin** is the ornamental stone pool where fountains play and children sail toy boats.

beau.etymology: Beau continues Latin bellus, pretty or graceful. The eleventh-century French form bel survives as a modern alternative before certain vowel sounds.

beaucoup.etymology: Beaucoup joins beau, formerly able to mean large, and coup, a portion cut from a whole. The Académie records thirteenth-century biau cop with the sense of a large and fine thing.

besoin.etymology: The Académie traces besoin probably to reconstructed Old Low Franconian *bisun(n)i, care or need. Thirteenth-century French had besoing. The proposed Germanic source is probable rather than certain.

beurre.etymology: Beurre comes from Latin butyrum, borrowed from Ancient Greek boútyron ('cow-cheese', from boûs 'cow' + tyrós 'cheese'), evolving through Old French burre into modern beurre.
beurre.notes: **Beurre doux** = unsalted butter; **beurre demi-sel / salé** = lightly salted / salted butter.

bibliothèque.etymology: Learned borrowing via Latin bibliotheca from Ancient Greek bibliothḗkē ('book repository, bookcase, library'), compounded from biblíon ('book, papyrus roll') and thḗkē ('case, chest, storage place', from tithénai 'to put').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: bibliothèque (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: bibliothèque

bibliothèque.notes: In French, **une bibliothèque** means both a public/private library AND a piece of furniture (a bookcase)—whereas **une librairie** is a bookshop.

bien.etymology: Bien descends from the Latin adverb bene, well. The Académie records it in French from the tenth century; the noun meaning a good or a possession developed from the adverb.

bientôt.etymology: Bientôt joins bien and tôt. Fourteenth-century bien tost meant in a short time, before the expression settled into its modern meaning soon.

biscuit.etymology: Compound inherited from Old French bescuit ('twice-baked bread'), modeled on Latin panis bis coctus: bis ('twice') + cuit (past participle of cuire 'to bake'). Originally it named dry, durable ship's bread baked a second time to drive out moisture.

history.meaning: crisp sweet cookie; light sponge cake

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: biscuit (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: biscuit

biscuit.notes: Ceramicists also call unglazed once-fired pottery **le biscuit** by analogy with dry baked biscuit.

blanc.etymology: Blanc entered Gallo-Romance from Frankish *blank ('shining, gleaming white', cognate with English 'blank'), displacing Classical Latin albus in everyday speech.
blanc.notes: Feminine **blanche** preserves the palatalised final consonant: *une nappe blanche*.

bois.etymology: Bois descends from Medieval Latin boscus ('woodland, timber'), probably of Germanic origin (akin to English 'bush'). It means both a small forest ('woods') and the material 'wood'.
bois.notes: **En bois** = made of wood (e.g. *un train en bois*, *un escalier en bois*).

bon.etymology: Bon descends from Latin bonus, good. The Académie records tenth-century French buon; forms such as feminine bonne belong to this same adjective.

bonjour.etymology: Bonjour joins bon and jour. The Académie records thirteenth-century bon jor with the sense of a good day or happy time. The wish developed into the familiar daytime greeting.
bonjour.notes: Use bonjour to greet someone during the day. Saying it when taking leave is regional; au revoir is the general farewell. Bonsoir is the usual evening greeting.

bouillon.etymology: Inherited from Old French boillon ('bubbling spring, boiling surge, broth'), derived from bouillir ('to boil') < Classical Latin bullire ('to bubble up'), itself from bulla ('water bubble').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from French bouillon and Old French boillir

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: bouillon (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: bouillon

bouillon.notes: In 19th-century Paris, affordable neighborhood restaurants serving hot beef **bouillon** to workers gave rise to the classic Parisian **Bouillon** dining halls.

boulanger.etymology: Continued from Old Northern French / Picard boulenc (12th century) and boulengier, most plausibly traced by Bloch-Wartburg and the TLFi to Middle Dutch bolle ('round loaf of bread', related to boule). In medieval towns a boulanger baked round loaves, gradually displacing the older French word talmelier.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: boulanger (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: boulanger

boulangerie.etymology: Derived in Middle French from boulanger ('baker'), earlier Picard and Old French boulenc / boulengier ('maker of round loaves'), borrowed from Middle Dutch or Old Picard bolle ('round ball-shaped loaf').

history.meaning: round loaf -> baker of round loaves

cognates.meaning: round loaf of country bread; ball

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: boulangerie (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: boulangerie

boulangerie.notes: Medieval French originally called a baker **talmelier** (from sifting flour); **boulanger** won out because customers prized plump round loaves.

boussole.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Italian bussola ('mariner's compass housed in a small boxwood case'), from Late Latin buxida ('little box made of boxwood'), altered from Greek pyxís (from pýxos 'box tree').

history.meaning: small box holding a magnetized needle

cognates.meaning: native inherited doublet from the same Late Latin buxida!
likewise ultimately from Late Latin buxus/buxis ('boxwood')

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: boussole (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: boussole

boussole.notes: Astonishingly, **une boussole** ('compass') and **une boîte** ('box') are etymological twins — a compass was named after the little boxwood case protecting its needle!

boîtier.etymology: Derived within French from boîte ('box') with the suffix -ier. Boîte itself goes back through Old French boiste to Late Latin buxida, from Greek pyxís ('small boxwood container', from pýxos 'box tree').

history.meaning: protective casing, watch case, junction box

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: boîtier (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: boîtier

brioche.etymology: Brioche appears in fifteenth-century Norman French, built on the dialect verb brier (Old French broier, 'to knead or pound dough with a wooden roller').
brioche.notes: **Une brioche à la cannelle** = a cinnamon roll/bun.

brique.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century via Picard/Flemish from Middle Dutch brike ('broken piece, flat cake, fired clay brick', related to breken 'to break').

cognates.meaning: borrowed in the 15th c. via French/Flemish
unrelated in form, whereas English break shares the Germanic root

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: brique (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: brique

brique.notes: In French culinary slang, rectangular milk or juice cartons are also called **des briques** (**une brique de lait**).

bristol.etymology: Shortened from papier bristol (early 19th century), named after the English port city of Bristol, whose paper mills became famous around 1800 for smooth, heavy pasted card stock (Bristol board).

history.meaning: fine calling card, index card, or recipe card

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: bristol (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)

bristol.notes: In France today, **une fiche bristol** (or simply **un bristol**) is every student's, librarian's, and baker's favorite sturdy index card.

buée.etymology: Derived from Old French buer ('to wash linen in steaming hot lye-ash water'), borrowed from Frankish *bukon ('to steep laundry in beech-ash lye'); the noun shifted from 'washhouse steam' to 'mist/condensation on cold glass'.

history.meaning: to soak linen in hot lye
vapor condensation on windows or glasses

cognates.meaning: to steep linen in hot lye

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: buée (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: buée

buée.notes: Unlike **vapeur** (steam rising in the air), **la buée** specifically names the fine mist that fogs a windowpane or a pair of spectacles.

cadeau.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century from Occitan capdel ('capital letter heading a chapter', from Latin capitellum 'little head'); calligraphers' ornate flourished capitals became 'festive flourishes / treats offered to please someone', and by the 18th century 'a gift'.

cognates.meaning: native northern French doublet from capitellum

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cadeau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: cadeau

cadeau.notes: Originally a calligrapher's decorative flourish added 'purely for pleasure rather than utility', **un cadeau** came to replace **un présent** in everyday French.

café.etymology: Café ultimately comes from Arabic qahwa through Turkish qahve. The Académie considers Italian caveé or caffè the probable intermediary into French. It records the seventeenth-century French spellings cauueh and cafeh.
café.notes:
- *Un café* in France is normally a small, strong espresso. For a milky coffee, ask for *un café crème* or *un café au lait*.
- The same word names both the drink and the place.

cahier.etymology: Cahier comes from Old French quayer, cayer, from Vulgar Latin *quaternium (Latin quaternio, 'gathering of four folded sheets', from quattuor 'four'). English 'quire' (of paper) comes from the exact same Old French word!
cahier.notes: Used for school exercise books and large bound ledgers.

calme.etymology: Calme entered Middle French via Italian calma ('stillness free of wind at sea'), ultimately from Late Latin cauma and Ancient Greek kaûma ('midday heat', when flocks and winds rest).
calme.notes: Both adjective (*une cour calme*) and masculine noun (*le calme*).

camionnette.etymology: Formed in late nineteenth-century French as the diminutive (-ette) of camion ('heavy dray cart, truck'), originally a Norman-Picard dialect word (camion, 14th c.) for a low transport dray.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: camionnette (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: camionnette

camomille.etymology: Borrowed via Medieval Latin camomilla from Ancient Greek khamaímēlon, literally 'ground-apple' (khamaí 'on the earth, low-growing' + mêlon 'apple'), because fresh chamomile blossoms give off a crisp scent of ripe apples.

cognates.meaning: chamomile (literally 'little apple', a calque of the Greek!)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: camomille (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: camomille

camomille.notes: Spanish **manzanilla** ('little apple') translates the Greek metaphor directly into Romance.

cannelle.etymology: Cannelle comes from Old French canele ('little reed or tube', diminutive of canne from Latin canna 'reed'), named after the rolled quill shape of dried cinnamon bark.
cannelle.notes: Italian *cannella* and Spanish *canela* share the exact same image of a rolled reed.

capitaine.etymology: Inherited from Old/Middle French capitaine, from Late Latin capitaneus ('prominent in size, chief, leader'), formed on Classical Latin caput, capitis ('head').

history.meaning: leader of a company or vessel

cognates.meaning: both borrowed from Old French forms of capitaneus
native doublet directly from Latin caput

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: capitaine (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: capitaine

capitaine.notes: **Chef** and **capitaine** both grow from Latin **caput** ('head'), one through popular Gallo-Romance sound change and the other through medieval administrative Latin.

capsule.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin capsula ('small box or coffer'), diminutive of capsa ('cylindrical box for papyrus rolls'), related to capere ('to hold, contain').

history.meaning: small sealed container, seed pod, time capsule

cognates.meaning: crate / reliquary box (doublets from Latin capsa)
borrowed via French from Latin capsula

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: capsule (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: capsule

capsule.notes: In everyday French, **une capsule** can mean a bottle cap, a coffee pod, a space capsule, or **une capsule temporelle** ('time capsule').

carotte.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Latin carota ('carrot'), itself from Ancient Greek karōtón, replacing the older medieval French name pastenade.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: carotte (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: carotte

carotte.notes: Notice the spelling contrast between French **carotte** (one *r*, two *t*'s) and English **carrot** (two *r*'s, one *t*).

carreau.etymology: Inherited from Old French quarrel ('four-sided block, square tile, crossbow bolt'), from Vulgar Latin quadrellum, diminutive of quadrum ('square', related to quattuor 'four'). From 'little square', it came to name both floor tiles and rectangular windowpanes.

history.meaning: tile; windowpane; check pattern; diamonds (in cards)

cognates.meaning: (archaic) square-headed crossbow bolt, from Old French quarrel

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: carreau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: carreau

carreau.notes: In everyday French, **faire les carreaux** means 'to wash the windows'.

carrière.etymology: In the career sense, carrière was borrowed from Old Provençal carriera, street, ultimately from a Latin expression for a road for carts. Its sixteenth-century French sense concerned a space for running horses. The quarry noun has a separate origin.

cartographe.etymology: Modern scholarly compound formed from carte ('map', from Latin charta 'sheet of papyrus') + -graphe (from Ancient Greek gráphein 'to draw, write, chart').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cartographe (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)

cartographe.notes: Note that French **une carte** covers 'map', 'postcard' (**carte postale**), 'menu/wine list', and 'playing card' all in a single word.

cause.etymology: Cause was borrowed from Latin causa, which could mean both a cause and a legal case. The Académie dates the French noun to the twelfth century.

cave.etymology: Cave comes from Latin cava ('hollow place, underground vault', feminine substantive of cavus 'hollow'). In French it denotes a cellar beneath a building (whereas an outdoor rock cave is une grotte).
cave.notes: False friend: **la cave** is a basement or wine cellar, not a wild mountainside cave (*une grotte*).

ce.etymology: Ce continues reconstructed Popular Latin *ecce hoc, a strengthened form of this. The tenth-century French form czo or ço weakened to ce when unstressed; c’ is its modern elided form.

celui.etymology: Celui and celle developed from strengthened Latin demonstrative forms, reconstructed as *ecce illui and *ecce illa(m). Tenth-century French had cels as an oblique masculine plural form.

cent.etymology: Cent descends from Latin centum, hundred. Its French use as a number is recorded from the tenth century; the unrelated monetary cent is a later borrowing from American English.

cercle.etymology: Inherited via Old French cercle from Classical Latin circulus ('circular figure, ring, orbit'), diminutive of circus ('ring, circular arena').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cercle (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: cercle

cercle.notes: In French pastry kitchens, **un cercle à tarte** is the bottomless metal pastry ring that gives bakery tarts crisp vertical edges.

chaise.etymology: Chaise originated as a fifteenth-century Parisian pronunciation variant of chaire (from Latin cathedra, Ancient Greek kathédra 'seat', where r and z swapped in speech). Chaire kept the elevated sense of 'pulpit, academic chair', while chaise became the everyday chair.

chaleur.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin calorem (accusative of calor, 'heat, warmth', from calere 'to be warm'). Regular Gallo-Romance palatalisation turned initial ca- before a into cha- (/ʃa/) and Latin -orem into French -eur.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: chaleur (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: chaleur

chaleur.notes: Latin abstract nouns in *-or* were masculine, which evolved into feminine nouns in French (**la chaleur**, **la couleur**, **la douleur**).

chambre.etymology: Chambre develops regularly from Latin camera ('vaulted ceiling, arched room', from Ancient Greek kamára). As k softened before a to ch and m-r developed a glide b, camera became Old French chambre ('room, bedroom').
chambre.notes: Chambre is specifically a bedroom or hotel room; a general room of a house or flat is **une pièce**.

chanson.etymology: Inherited from Spoken Latin cantionem (accusative of cantio, 'singing, song, incantation', from canere / cantare 'to sing'). Before a, Latin c- shifted to ch- and -tio- became -son.

history.meaning: sung poem, song (as in chanson de geste)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: chanson (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: chanson

chapeau.etymology: Inherited from Old French chapel ('wreath of flowers, hood, hat'), from Vulgar Latin cappellum, diminutive of Late Latin cappa ('hooded cloak, cape').

history.meaning: hooded cape -> little hood, head covering
garland or hat worn on the head

cognates.meaning: from Old French chapelet and Late Latin cappa

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: chapeau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: chapeau

chapeau.notes: Tipping one's hat in respect gave French the standalone exclamation **Chapeau!** ('Hats off! Well done!').

chariot.etymology: Formed in Old French with suffix -ot from charriier / char ('wheeled cart'), inherited from Gallo-Latin carrus ('four-wheeled Celtic wagon'), itself from Gaulish *karros.

history.meaning: trolley, book cart, luggage or pastry cart

cognates.meaning: all borrowed through Old/Anglo-Norman French from carrus

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: chariot (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: chariot

chariot.notes: Note that traditional French spells **chariot** with a single *-r-* (unlike **charrette** and **charrier**), though the 1990 spelling recommendations also allow *charriot*.

charnière.etymology: From Old French charniere ('hinge, pivot, joint'), formed on Spoken Latin *cardinaria from Classical Latin cardo, cardinis ('door pivot, hinge, axis'—the same Latin root that gave English cardinal, originally 'pivotal').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: charnière (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: charnière

chaud.etymology: Chaud comes from Latin calidus (syncopated in spoken Latin to caldus, 'warm, hot'): initial ca- became cha- and l before d vocalised to u, giving Old French chalt, chaud.

chaussure.etymology: Chaussure derives from Old French chauceüre, built on chausser ('to put on shoes or hose'), ultimately from Latin calceare and calceus ('shoe', from calx 'heel').
chaussure.notes: Paired with **chausser** (*chausser du 40* = to wear size 40 shoes).

cher.etymology: Cher comes from Latin carus, which already had both the senses beloved and costly. The Académie records the French adjective from the tenth century.

chercher.etymology: Chercher descends from Late Latin circare ('to go around, patrol, search everywhere', from circus 'circle'). Old French cerchier gave English 'search' while assimilating in French to chercher.
chercher.notes: No preposition for 'for': **chercher ses clés** = 'to look for one's keys'.

cheville.etymology: Inherited via Old French cheville ('wooden peg, pin') from Vulgar Latin clavicula ('little key, peg, bolt'), diminutive of Classical Latin clavis ('key'). Because the anklebone juts out on either side of the foot like a rounded wooden peg, cheville became the standard French word for 'ankle'.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cheville (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: cheville

cheville.notes: Luthiers still call violin and guitar tuning pegs **les chevilles**.

chose.etymology: Chose descends from Latin causa. In later everyday Latin, the word expanded from cause or case to the broad meaning thing, replacing uses of res. The French form is recorded from the ninth century.

chuchoter.etymology: Expressive verb attested since the 16th century (earlier chucheter), formed on the hushed onomatopoeia chut / chu-chu imitating soft sibilant whispering.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: chuchoter (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: chuchoter

chuchoter.notes: Say **chuchoter** **/ʃyʃɔte/** aloud and its two */ʃ/* sounds literally sound like two people whispering in a quiet library!

cire.etymology: Inherited via Old French cire from Classical Latin cera ('beeswax, wax writing tablet, wax seal'), cognate with Ancient Greek kērós ('beeswax').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cire (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: cire

cire.notes: Rubbing linen with melted **cire** to waterproof it gave French **la toile cirée** ('oilcloth / waxed cloth') and the fisherman's yellow **ciré** raincoat.

citron.etymology: Citron derives from Latin citrus ('citron tree'), extended with -on in French to name the yellow lemon (whereas English 'citron' kept the older sense of a thick-rind citrus fruit).
citron.notes: False friend in reverse: French **citron** is an everyday yellow lemon; a green lime is **un citron vert**.

citronnier.etymology: Formed within French from citron ('lemon', from Latin citrum) plus the productive tree-naming suffix -ier (from Latin -arius).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: citronnier (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: citronnier

client.etymology: Client was borrowed from Latin cliens, clientis ('follower under a patron's protection'), expanding in modern French to mean a customer, hotel guest, or professional client.
client.notes: In a hotel, **un client / une cliente** means a hotel guest.

clignoter.etymology: Frequentative verb formed in Middle French from cligner ('to blink, wink, half-close the eyes') with the iterative suffix -oter ('to do repeatedly in small bursts'). Cligner descends from Spoken Latin *cliniare, related to clinare ('to incline, lower').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: clignoter (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: clignoter

cloche.etymology: Cloche comes from Medieval Latin clocca ('bell'), a word spread across Europe by early Irish missionary monks (Old Irish cloc 'bell', ultimately imitative of ringing). English 'clock' comes from the exact same root!
cloche.notes: Diminutive **la clochette** = small handbell or gate bell.

clochette.etymology: Diminutive in -ette of cloche ('bell'), from Merovingian/Medieval Latin clocca ('handbell'), spread across Western Europe by early Irish missionary monks (compare Old Irish cloc 'bell').

cognates.meaning: originally a bell-striking timepiece, from the same clocca word

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: clochette (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: clochette

clochette.notes: Because early mechanical tower clocks had no dials and announced hours purely by ringing a bell, Medieval Latin **clocca** gave French **cloche** ('bell') and English **clock**.

clé.etymology: Clé (also spelled clef) comes from Latin clavis ('key, bolt'), related to claudere ('to close'). Final v dropped in spoken French while spelling preserved -f in clef until modern clé became standard.
clé.notes: **Fermer à clé** = to lock; **sous clé** = under lock and key.

clôture.etymology: Inherited via Old French closture from Late Latin claustura ('barrier, enclosure, fastening'), formed on claudere, clausum ('to shut, close').

cognates.meaning: from sister formations on Latin claudere

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: clôture (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: clôture

clôture.notes: Once again, the circumflex in **clôture** preserves the memory of the vanished *-s-* in Old French **closture**.

colline.etymology: Borrowed in the sixteenth century from Italian collina ('gentle hill'), derived from Classical Latin collis ('hill', adjective collinus 'of a hill').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: colline (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: colline

colline.notes: Lyon is traditionally described through its two famous **collines**: Fourvière (*la colline qui prie*) and la Croix-Rousse (*la colline qui travaille*).

comme.etymology: Comme developed from Latin quomodo, in what way, through later quomo. Early French had cum and com; com remained in use into the sixteenth century.

compter.etymology: Compter comes from Latin computare, to calculate. French originally wrote conter; an etymological spelling with p became associated with counting, while conter retained the storytelling sense.

comptoir.etymology: From Old French comptoir / conteoir ('counting room, counting table'), formed on compter ('to count, reckon', from Latin computare) + the place/instrument suffix -oir (Latin -atorium). Originally the merchant's table where coins were tallied.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: comptoir (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: comptoir

confiance.etymology: Confiance was borrowed from Latin confidentia, trust, related to confidere. The Académie records thirteenth-century confience.

content.etymology: Content comes from Latin contentus, satisfied, the past participle of continere, to contain or hold within. The French adjective is recorded from the thirteenth century.

contrôle.etymology: Contracted from Old and Middle French contrerolle ('duplicate parchment roll kept to verify an original tax or accounting register'), compound of contre ('against, alongside') + rôle ('scroll, roll' < Latin rotulus).

history.meaning: verification, inspection; later also 'mastery' via English

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: contrôle (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: contrôle

contrôle.notes: This origin explains a classic French-English false friend: **un contrôle** in French usually means a 'check, inspection, or ticket check' (**liste de contrôle** = checklist), not domination.

corail.etymology: Inherited via Old French coral / corail from Classical Latin corallium, borrowed from Ancient Greek korállion ('red Mediterranean coral').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: corail (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: corail

corail.notes: When used as a noun for reef coral, the plural is **des coraux**, whereas as a color modifier (**des lentilles corail**, 'red lentils') **corail** stays invariable.

corde.etymology: Inherited from Latin chorda ('catgut string of a lyre or harp, cord'), borrowed from Ancient Greek khordḗ ('gut string of a musical instrument'). The musical sense is actually the oldest meaning of the word, older than 'rope'!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: corde (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: corde

corde.notes: From Latin *accordare* (originally debated between *cor* 'heart' and *chorda* 'tuning strings together') comes **accorder un piano**.

coton.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century (via Italian cotone during Mediterranean trade) from Arabic quṭn / quṭun ('cotton').

cognates.meaning: borrowed directly from Andalusi Arabic al-quṭún (keeping article al-)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: coton (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: coton

coton.notes: Compare French **coton** (via Italian, without the Arabic article) and Spanish **algodón** (which kept Arabic **al-** 'the').

couloir.etymology: Formed from couler ('to flow, glide through', from Latin colare 'to strain, filter, flow') + -oir. Originally a strainer or narrow channel for liquids, by the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries un couloir came to mean a narrow indoor passageway through which people move from room to room.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: couloir (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: couloir

couper.etymology: Couper is derived from coup, a blow. Its early literal sense was dividing something with a blow; the verb is recorded from the eleventh century.

cour.etymology: Cour descends from Popular Latin *curtis (from Classical Latin cohors, cohortis, 'enclosed yard, farmyard, retinue'). It denoted both an enclosed courtyard and a ruler's court; the dropped final t was never restored in spelling (unlike court 'short' from curtus).
cour.notes: **Donner sur la cour** = to overlook the courtyard (prized in French apartments and hotels for quiet).

cours.etymology: Cours descends from Latin cursus, the action of running. Its extended senses include a course or sequence of study. This is distinct from the later specialised noun for a broad avenue.

coussin.etymology: Inherited from Old French coissin / coussin, from Vulgar Latin *coxinum ('seat pad for the hips'), derived from Classical Latin coxa ('hip', which itself evolved into French cuisse 'thigh').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: coussin (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: coussin

coussin.notes: Contrast **un coussin** (seat or sofa cushion) with **un oreiller** (bed pillow, from *oreille* 'ear').

couvercle.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin cooperculum ('cover, lid'), an instrument noun built on cooperire ('to cover completely'—the same verb that gave French couvrir and English cover).

history.meaning: lid of a vessel or chest

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: couvercle (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: couvercle

craie.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin creta ('chalk, fine white clay, fuller's earth'). Regular loss of intervocalic -t- and diphthongisation of long ē turned creta into Old French creie, then craie.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: craie (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: craie

craie.notes: English **crayon** was borrowed from French *crayon*, originally 'a small stick of **craie** (chalk)'.

cravate.etymology: Adopted in the mid-17th century as a phonetic adaptation of Croate ('Croatian'), naming the knotted linen neck-scarves worn by Croatian light horsemen serving in King Louis XIII and Louis XIV's Royal-Cravates regiment.

history.meaning: scarf knotted around the collar; necktie

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cravate (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: cravate

cravate.notes: Croatia celebrates International Cravat Day every October in honor of how **la cravate** traveled from Croatian riders through Paris to wardrobes worldwide.

crayon.etymology: Crayon was formed in French from craie ('chalk', from Latin creta) + -on, originally meaning a piece of drawing chalk before naming the graphite pencil.
crayon.notes: False friend: **un crayon** is an ordinary pencil (*écrire au crayon* = 'write in pencil').

crochet.etymology: Diminutive formed in Old French from croc ('hook, curved fang') + -et, with croc borrowed from Frankish *krōk or Old Norse krókr ('hook').

cognates.meaning: hooked needlework (from French); curved staff (from Norse)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: crochet (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: crochet

crochet.notes: English borrowed **crochet** directly from French because the yarn is worked with a small hooked needle.

croquis.etymology: Derived in the mid-18th century from the verb croquer ('to crunch', and figuratively among 17th-century painters 'to dash off or capture a subject briskly in a few strokes'), with suffix -is.

morphemes.meaning: result of an action (compare gâchis, fouillis)

cognates.meaning: borrowed in fashion and art drawing from French

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: croquis (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: croquis

croquis.notes: What a vivid studio metaphor: **un croquis** is a drawing 'bitten off' briskly from real life before the moment passes!

cuisson.etymology: Inherited from Old French cuisson, from Vulgar Latin *coctionem (Classical Latin coctio, coctionis 'cooking, baking'), action noun of coquere ('to cook, bake').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cuisson (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: cuisson

cuisson.notes: Whether asking how you'd like a steak cooked (**Quelle cuisson?**) or timing a brioche in the oven (**le temps de cuisson**), **la cuisson** is essential French kitchen vocabulary.

cuivre.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin cuprum (shortened from aes Cyprium, 'metal of Cyprus', because the island of Cyprus had the Roman world's chief copper mines). Cuprum yielded Old French cuevre / cuivre—just as it gave English copper.

cognates.meaning: copper (early Germanic borrowing from Latin cuprum)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cuivre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: cuivre

céramique.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries from Ancient Greek keramikḗ (tékhnē) ('the potter's art'), from kéramos ('potter's clay, earthenware jar'), which also named the Kerameikós potters' quarter of ancient Athens.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: céramique (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: céramique

céramique.notes: Covers earthenware (**la faïence**), stoneware (**le grès**), and porcelain (**la porcelaine**).

d'accord.etymology: This expression combines the elided preposition de with accord, agreement. Accord itself is a noun formed from accorder. In the fixed expression, the combination expresses being in agreement.

dalle.etymology: Originally a Norman maritime and building word dale ('deck scupper trough; grooved flagstone channeled for rainwater; flat paving slab'), borrowed from Old Norse dœla ('small wooden gutter or trough aboard ship', related to dalr 'valley, hollow').

cognates.meaning: from related Old Norse dalr / Old English dæl ('valley')

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: dalle (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: dalle

dalle.notes: From Viking ship gutters in Normandy to cathedral and courtyard flagstones across France, **une dalle** traveled a remarkable journey.

dame.etymology: Inherited via Old French dame from Classical Latin domina ('mistress of a household, lady'), feminine counterpart of dominus ('master, lord', from domus 'house').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: dame (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: dame

dame.notes: **Madame** is simply the fused possessive phrase *ma dame* ('my lady').

dans.etymology: Dans comes from later Latin deintus, inside, composed from an intensive de- and intus, within. The Académie dates its French history to the twelfth century.

de.etymology: De continues the Latin preposition de. Its older senses included separation and origin; later everyday Latin also expanded its use in partitive and possessive relationships. French inherited those connecting uses.

demain.etymology: Demain developed from the later Latin expression de mane. That expression could refer to the morning and also to the morning of the following day; the latter reading became tomorrow.

demander.etymology: Demander comes from Latin demandare ('to entrust', and in Late Latin 'to request, ask for'). Unlike English 'demand', French demander is the polite everyday verb 'to ask'.

history.meaning: to entrust; Late Latin: to request

demander.notes: False friend: **demander** simply means 'to ask' (not 'demand', which is *exiger*).

dernier.etymology: Dernier is a fifteenth-century contraction of derrenier, itself related to an older form ultimately derived from Latin deretro, behind. Its history connects being last with being at the back.

deux.etymology: Deux continues Latin duos, an object-case form of duo, two. The Académie records earlier French dos, dous and deus before the spelling deux.

deuxième.etymology: Deuxième was formed from deux ('two', from Latin duos) + the ordinal suffix -ième, providing a regular ordinal alongside older second.
deuxième.notes: Used interchangeably with *second(e)*, and preferred whenever a third (*troisième*) exists.

devoir.etymology: Devoir comes from Latin debere, to owe or be indebted. Its French use to express obligation is recorded from the ninth century. The noun meaning duty developed from the verb.

dire.etymology: Dire continues Latin dicere, meaning to say or express something in words. The Académie dates the French verb to the tenth century. Declaring, naming and recounting are extensions of that central meaning.
dire.notes:
- Irregular: the *vous* form is *dites*, not *disez* (also *vous redites*, but *vous contredisez*).
- *Dire* is used with indirect speech: *dire que* + clause.

dix.etymology: Dix descends from Latin decem, ten. Eleventh-century French spellings included dis and diz.

dormir.etymology: Dormir continues Latin dormire, to sleep. The Académie records the French verb from the twelfth century.

douzaine.etymology: Formed in twelfth-century Old French (dozaine) from douze ('twelve', Latin duodecim) plus the collective numeral suffix -aine (from Latin -ena). English dozen was borrowed directly from Old French dozaine.

cognates.meaning: group of twelve (from Old French dozaine)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: douzaine (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: douzaine

du.etymology: Du is the contraction of de and the masculine singular article le. The ninth-century form del shows an earlier stage of the combination. Modern uses depend on whether the phrase expresses a relationship or an unspecified quantity.

dé.etymology: In the sense of 'gaming die' and 'small cube' (un dé de carotte), inherited via Old French dé from Classical Latin datum ('that which is given or cast', neuter past participle of dare 'to give, throw'), used in Roman gaming slang for throwing dice.

history.meaning: something given or thrown (a cast of the dice)
die; small culinary cube (couper en dés)

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French dé / dés

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: dé (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: dé

dé.notes: Homonym note: **un dé à coudre** ('thimble') has a completely different origin—from Latin *digitale* ('finger cap', from *digitus* 'finger')!

décès.etymology: Décès was borrowed from Latin decessus, departure or death. The Académie records the French word from the eleventh century.

déjeuner.etymology: Déjeuner developed from a reconstructed Popular Latin verb *disjunare, shortened from *disjejunare, breaking a fast. Twelfth-century French used a reflexive form for taking the morning meal; in modern metropolitan French the usual meal is lunch.

désolé.etymology: Désolé is the past participle of désoler, also used as an adjective. The Académie traces the verb to Latin desolare, to depopulate or devastate. The everyday apology uses a milder sense of distress or regret.

eau.etymology: Eau descends intact through speech from Latin aqua ('water')! Intervocalic -qu- softened and dropped, leaving Old French ewe, eaue, modern eau — five Latin letters transformed into three vowels pronounced simply /o/.
eau.notes: **Eau chaude / froide** = hot / cold water; **eau gazeuse** = sparkling water.

elle.etymology: Elle continues Latin illa, the feminine of the demonstrative ille, that one. The Académie records ninth-century ele as a subject form and thirteenth-century elle as an object form. Modern elle can therefore be understood against a history with different grammatical uses and spellings.

embouteillage.etymology: Derived from embouteiller ('to pour wine into bottles', from en- + bouteille 'bottle' < Late Latin butticula 'small cask'); applied figuratively in Paris around the 1890s–1900s to vehicles wedged into a narrow street like liquid in a bottleneck.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: embouteillage (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)

embouteillage.notes: Colloquial French carries the wine-bottle pun one step further by calling a traffic jam **un bouchon** ('a cork')!

en.etymology: As a preposition, en descends from Latin in. It survives in many old fixed expressions, even where dans now serves other location senses. The pronoun en has a different Latin source, inde, from there.

encore.etymology: Encore is traced to a reconstructed Popular Latin expression *hinc ha hora or *hinc ad horam, approximately from here until this hour. The French word is recorded from the eleventh century.

encre.etymology: Inherited from Old French enque / encre, from Late Latin encaustum ('purple ink used by Roman emperors'), borrowed from Ancient Greek énkauston ('burned in, heat-prepared pigment', from enkaíein 'to burn in') with proparoxytonic stress shift.

cognates.meaning: ink was borrowed from Old French enque

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: encre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: encre

encre.notes: English **ink** comes straight from the older Old French form **enque**, before French inserted an *-r-* to give **encre**.

envoyer.etymology: Envoyer continues later Latin inviare, to travel along or reach a place, which also developed the sense send. The French verb is recorded from the tenth century.

erreur.etymology: Erreur comes from Latin error, errorem ('wandering astray, mistake', from errare 'to wander, err'). Like most Latin abstract nouns in -or, it became feminine in French.
erreur.notes: **Par erreur** = by mistake; **mon erreur** uses *mon* before a vowel despite feminine gender.

escalier.etymology: Borrowed in the sixteenth century from Old Provençal escalier (from Late Latin scalarium, built on scala 'ladder, flight of steps'). Earlier French used degré or montée; notice the prosthetic e- before sc- (compare scala -> échelle).
escalier.notes: **Monter / descendre l'escalier** = to go upstairs / downstairs.

et.etymology: Et continues the Latin conjunction et, and. French had the ninth-century form e before the spelling was remodelled in the twelfth century; the written final t is not pronounced in the conjunction.

excuser.etymology: Excuser was borrowed from Latin excusare, to remove from blame, justify or excuse. The Académie records it from the twelfth century.

facteur.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Latin factor ('maker, doer, creator', agent noun of facere 'to make, do'); first used in French for an artisan maker of musical instruments (facteur de pianos) and commercial agent, then in the 19th century for a mail carrier.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: facteur (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: facteur

facteur.notes: Remarkably, both Odette's world and the hotel's mail share this word: a piano builder is still called **un facteur de pianos**, while the person delivering postcards is **le facteur**.

faire.etymology: Faire continues Latin facere, to do or make. The Académie dates the French verb to the ninth century. Both creating something and carrying out an action belong to its central meaning, which is why English may use either make or do depending on the construction.

fait.etymology: Fait comes regularly from Latin factum ('deed, thing done', neuter past participle of facere 'to do, make'), with Latin -ct- developing to French -it.
fait.notes: **En fait** = in fact, actually; **tout à fait** = quite, completely.

fantastique.etymology: Fantastique was borrowed through later Latin fantasticus from Greek phantastikos, capable of forming images or imagining illusions. The French adjective is recorded from the fourteenth century.

fenêtre.etymology: Fenêtre comes from Latin fenestra ('window, opening for light'). The circumflex over ê marks the Old French s that disappeared before t (compare English 'defenestrate').
fenêtre.notes: **Regarder par la fenêtre** = to look out through the window.

fer-blanc.etymology: Compound attested since the 16th century from fer ('iron' < Classical Latin ferrum) + blanc ('white, gleaming bright' < Frankish *blank), naming thin sheet iron dipped in molten tin so it gleams silvery-white and resists rust.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: fer-blanc (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: fer-blanc

fer-blanc.notes: Classic French biscuit tins, tea caddies, and childhood keepsake boxes are traditionally made of **fer-blanc**.

feutre.etymology: Inherited via Old French feltre from West Germanic / Frankish *filtir ('pressed wool, felt'). Medieval Latin Latinized this same Germanic word as filtrum—giving French filtre and English filter, because liquids were strained through pads of wool felt!

cognates.meaning: native Germanic cognate / Medieval Latin derivative

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: feutre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: feutre

feutre.notes: From *feutre* also comes the adjective **feutré** ('muffled, hushed', like footsteps on felt or a felt piano hammer).

ficelle.etymology: Inherited from Old French ficele ('thin cord, string'), from Vulgar Latin *fiscella (Classical Latin fiscella 'small basket woven of slender rushes', crossed in Gallo-Romance with filum 'thread').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: ficelle (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: ficelle

ficelle.notes: In French bakeries, **une ficelle** is also a slender, extra-crisp cousin of the **baguette**, half as wide and twice as crunchy.

fiche.etymology: Deverbal noun from ficher ('to drive in, fix, pin fast'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *figicare, frequentative of Classical Latin figere ('to fasten, pierce'); shifted from a peg/slip pinned onto a board to a catalog or recipe card.

history.meaning: index card, catalog slip, recipe card

cognates.meaning: microfiche borrowed directly from French fiche

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: fiche (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: fiche

fiche.notes: Notice the family resemblance between **une fiche** (a card slipped into a file) and **une affiche** (a notice posted on a wall)!

film.etymology: Film is a nineteenth-century borrowing from English film, originally a membrane or thin covering. The material sense provided the name for the photographic medium and later for the work recorded on it.

flèche.etymology: From twelfth-century Old French fleche ('arrow'), generally traced via Old Low Franconian *fliugika ('flying shaft', related to Germanic *fleugan 'to fly'). Extended to church spires and later to drawn directional pointers.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: flèche (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: flèche

fois.etymology: Fois continues Latin vices, turns or alternations, the plural of an otherwise unused form reconstructed as *vix. Tenth-century French had feiz. The modern word counts occurrences.

formidable.etymology: Formidable was borrowed from Latin formidabilis, inspiring fear, related to formido, terror. The French word originally concerned something frightening before developing its familiar favourable sense.

forêt.etymology: Inherited from Old French forest, from Carolingian Medieval Latin (silva) forestis ('unenclosed royal woodland lying outside park walls'), derived from Classical Latin foris ('outdoors, outside').

history.meaning: open royal woodland outside fenced enclosures

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: forêt (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: forêt

forêt.notes: The circumflex in **forêt** preserves the memory of the *s* still pronounced in **forestier** ('forestry') and English *forest*.

fouetter.etymology: Derived in Middle French from fouet ('whip, whisk'), itself the diminutive of Old French fou ('beech tree', from Latin fagus), because a fouet was originally a supple thin beech switch!

morphemes.meaning: beech tree (Old French fou < Latin fagus)

history.meaning: to whip; to whisk cream or eggs

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: fouetter (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: fouetter

fouetter.notes: In a French kitchen, the wire balloon whisk itself is simply called **un fouet**.

four.etymology: Four descends from Latin furnus ('oven, furnace') via Old French forn, four; final n dropped after r (though derivatives like fourneau and boulanger's fournil kept the n).
four.notes: **Sorti du four** = fresh out of the oven.

fourneau.etymology: Inherited from Old French fornel ('small oven, hearth, stove'), diminutive of four ('oven', from Classical Latin furnus).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: fourneau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: fourneau

fourneau.notes: To be busy cooking for guests is idiomatically **être aux fourneaux**.

fredonner.etymology: Derived in sixteenth-century French from fredon ('musical trill, vocal ornament, refrain'), an expressive onomatopoeic formation imitating rapid hummed notes.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: fredonner (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: fredonner

froid.etymology: Froid descends from Popular Latin *frigidus / *frigdu ('cold', Classical Latin frigidus). Loss of the unstressed vowel and palatalisation of -gd- produced Old French freit, froit, modern froid.
froid.notes: **Avoir froid** = to feel cold (of a person); **refroidir** = to cool down.

fromage.etymology: Fromage comes from Late Latin *(caseus) formaticus — 'cheese shaped in a mould' (from forma 'mould, form'). Through metathesis of r, Old French formage became modern fromage, while Italian formaggio kept the original order.
fromage.notes: Same Latin phrase gave Italian *formaggio* and Catalan *formatge*.

frère.etymology: Frère descends from Latin frater, fratrem ('brother'), with regular lenition of intervocalic -tr- to -r- through Old French frere.
frère.notes: **Grand frère / petit frère** = older / younger brother.

fusain.etymology: Inherited via Old French fusain ('spindle tree') from Vulgar Latin *fusago, *fusaginem, derived from Classical Latin fusus ('spinning spindle'), because its dense fine wood was prized first for carving spindles and later for charring into artists' charcoal sticks.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: fusain (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: fusain

fusain.notes: Even when modern charcoal sticks are made from willow twigs, French artists still call every charcoal drawing **un dessin au fusain**.

fusible.etymology: Originally a fourteenth-century learned adjective from Medieval Latin fusibilis ('capable of melting', from fundere, fusum 'to melt, pour'). In late nineteenth-century electricity, un coupe-circuit fusible was shortened to un fusible: the calibrated wire designed to melt first and protect the circuit.

history.meaning: safety fuse in an electrical circuit

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: fusible (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: fusible

gant.etymology: Inherited from Old French guant / gant, borrowed from Frankish *want ('glove, hand-wrapping', related to Germanic *windan 'to wind, wrap around').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French gantelet ('little/armored glove')

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: gant (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: gant

gant.notes: Initial Frankish *w-* regularly became *gu-* -> *g-* in French (just as *wardon* gave **garder** and *werra* gave **guerre**).

gare.etymology: Gare originally meant a sheltered river dock where boats pulled aside (from garer 'to moor, shelter', of Frankish origin *waron 'to watch out, protect'). In the railway age, river-dock terminology transferred directly to train stations!
gare.notes: For bus or tram stops, French says **un arrêt**; for metro, **une station**; for trains, **la gare**.

gauche.etymology: Gauche emerged in Middle French, probably from gauchir ('to veer aside, bend', from Frankish *wenkjan 'to waveringly turn aside', cognate with English 'wink' and 'flinch'), replacing older senestre ('left').

gond.etymology: Inherited via Old French gont from Late Latin gumphus / gomphus ('iron hinge pin, peg, joint'), borrowed from Ancient Greek gómphos ('wooden peg, iron bolt, molar tooth').

history.meaning: vertical iron pintle supporting a door or shutter

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: gond (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: gond

gond.notes: Because a shutter lifted off its *gonds* swings out of control, **sortir de ses gonds** means 'to lose one's temper'—literally 'to come off one's hinges'!

grand.etymology: Grand comes from Latin grandis ('full-grown, tall, great'), which completely displaced Classical Latin magnus in spoken Gallo-Romance.
grand.notes: Before a vowel or mute h, liaison sounds final d as /t/ (*un grand hôtel* /ɛ̃ ɡʁɑ̃t‿otɛl/).

grenier.etymology: Grenier descends from Latin granarium ('granary, grain loft above a house', from granum 'grain'). Because grain was stored dry under the rafters, le grenier became the everyday word for an attic.
grenier.notes: Compare English 'granary' and 'garner' (borrowed from Old French).

grès.etymology: From twelfth-century Old French gres ('gritstone, sandstone, cobblestone'), borrowed from Old Low Franconian *greot ('coarse sand, gravel'—cognate with Old English greot, modern English grit). Later applied to dense, high-fired stoneware pottery whose vitrified body is as hard as sandstone.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: grès (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: grès

guêpe.etymology: Guêpe developed from reconstructed Gallo-Romance *wespa, a blend of Latin vespa and Frankish *waspa, both meaning wasp. The Académie records twelfth-century wespe.

gâteau.etymology: Gâteau descends from Old French gastel ('fine round loaf, cake'), borrowed from Frankish *wastil ('food, pastry'). As s before t fell silent and vocalised -el became -eau, gastel became gâteau (compare English 'wastel-bread').

génial.etymology: Génial was borrowed from Latin genialis, associated with birth or festivity and related to genius. Its sixteenth-century French senses included fruitful or pleasant, before its modern uses for brilliance or enthusiastic approval.

heure.etymology: Heure continues Latin hora, hour, a borrowing from Greek hôra, a period of time. The Académie records the eleventh-century French form ure. The word’s earlier history concerns a period or division of time, rather than only the modern clock display.

histoire.etymology: Histoire was borrowed from Latin historia (from Ancient Greek historía 'inquiry, narrative, account'). Mute h triggers elision and liaison: *l'histoire*, *mon histoire*.

horloge.etymology: Horloge descends via Old French orloge from Latin horologium and Ancient Greek hōrológion ('instrument that tells the hour', from hṓra 'hour' + légein 'to tell').
horloge.notes: Mute h: **l'horloge** (feminine), unlike a wristwatch (**une montre**).

horloger.etymology: Agent noun formed in Middle French from horloge ('clock') + -er, with horloge coming via Latin horologium from Ancient Greek hōrológion ('hour-teller', from hṓra 'hour' + légein 'to tell, read out').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: horloger (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: horloger

horloger.notes: Unlike *hêtre*, the *h* in **l'horloger** and **l'horloge** is Latin-Greek and completely mute.

huile.etymology: Inherited via Old French oile / uile from Classical Latin oleum ('olive oil'), borrowed from Ancient Greek élaion (from elaía 'olive tree'). Medieval French scribes added a silent initial h- purely so manuscript readers would not misread uile as vile ('vile, cheap'), since u and v were written with the same letter!

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French oile before graphic h- was added

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: huile (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: huile

huile.notes: The exact same scribal trick explains silent *h-* in **huit** (*uit* vs *vit*), **huître** (*uistre* 'oyster'), and **huis** (*uis* 'door', as in *à huis clos*)!

hêtre.etymology: Borrowed via Old and Middle French hestre from Frankish *haistr ('young beech sapling', compare Middle Dutch heester). It gradually replaced Old French fou (< Latin fagus) because fou had become homophonous with fou ('mad, crazy')!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: hêtre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: hêtre

hêtre.notes: Because it comes from Germanic rather than Latin, **le hêtre** keeps an *h* aspiré (never *l'hêtre*!).

hôtel.etymology: Hôtel descends from Medieval Latin hospitale ('guest quarters, hostel'), neuter substantive of hospitalis ('relating to a guest or host', from hospes). Old French ostel meant a lodging or town residence; the circumflex in hôtel marks the lost s that English kept in hostel and hospital.
hôtel.notes: Compare **hôtel de ville** ('town hall') and **hôpital** (learned doublet from the same Latin root).

ici.etymology: Ici combines an initial element from Old French iluec, there, with ci. The Académie dates the word to the eleventh century.

idée.etymology: Idée continues Latin idea, borrowed from Greek idea, visible form, kind or category, related to the Greek verb for seeing. The Académie records the twelfth-century French form idees.

il.etymology: Il developed from later Latin pronoun forms illi and illum, continuing Classical Latin ille and illud, that person or that thing. The Académie dates the French pronoun to the ninth century. A demonstrative used to point something out became a third-person subject pronoun.

improviser.etymology: Improviser is a seventeenth-century borrowing from Italian improvvisare, with the same sense of producing something without prior preparation.

impôt.etymology: Inherited from Old French impost, from Medieval/Classical Latin impositum ('assessment or charge laid upon', substantivized neuter past participle of imponere 'to place upon').

history.meaning: to lay upon -> charge laid upon

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Middle French impost / imposer

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: impôt (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: impôt

impôt.notes: As always in French spelling, the circumflex on **impôt** marks the historical *-s-* of Old French **impost**.

indice.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin indicium ('disclosing sign, token, proof'), related to index ('forefinger, pointer') and indicare ('to point out, make known').

history.meaning: to point out -> revealing sign, clue

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: indice (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: indice

indice.notes: False-friend alert: English *index* (at the back of a book) is **un index** in French too, whereas **un indice** primarily means a 'clue' or 'revealing sign'!

interrupteur.etymology: Adapted in nineteenth-century physics and electrical engineering from Latin interruptor ('one who breaks off', from interrumpere 'to break between, interrupt'): a switch opens or closes a gap in the electrical current.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: interrupteur (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: interrupteur

itinéraire.etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin itinerarium ('road map, travel account'), derived from Classical Latin iter, itineris ('walk, road, journey', related to ire 'to go').

cognates.meaning: from the same Late Latin stem

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: itinéraire (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: itinéraire

itinéraire.notes: On French road signs, **Itinéraire bis** marks a scenic or secondary detour route avoiding holiday traffic!

ivoire.etymology: Inherited through Old French ivurie / ivoire from Latin eboreus ('made of ivory', from ebur 'ivory'—itself borrowed via Egyptian ābu 'elephant, ivory').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: ivoire (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: ivoire

jamais.etymology: Jamais combines Old French ja ('already, ever', from Latin iam) + mais ('more', from Latin magis): literally 'ever more'. Paired with ne, it came to mean 'never'.
jamais.notes: Without *ne* in questions (*Si jamais...*), it can still mean 'ever'.

jardin.etymology: Jardin comes from Gallo-Roman *hortus gardinus ('enclosed garden'), built on Frankish *gardo ('enclosure, yard', cognate with English 'yard' and 'garden'). Old French jardin passed straight into English 'garden' via Norman.

je.etymology: Je descends from Late Latin eo, itself continuing Classical Latin ego, I. The Académie dates the French pronoun to the eleventh century. Its earlier Latin forms help explain a history that is not obvious from the very short modern word.

jeudi.etymology: Jeudi developed from Latin Jovis dies, day of Jupiter. The Académie records the twelfth-century form juesdi.

journée.etymology: Journée is derived from jour, day. The twelfth-century form journee already belongs to this French word family.

jusque.etymology: Jusque descends from Latin inde usque ('from there all the way to'), blending de + usque ('all the way, continuously') into Old French jusque, jusques.
jusque.notes: Usually elides before *à* or *au*: **jusqu'à demain**, **jusqu'au deuxième étage**.

juste.etymology: Juste was borrowed from Latin justus, just or right. The adjective is recorded from the twelfth century; adverbial uses such as just or only developed alongside it.

lait.etymology: Lait comes from Popular Latin *lacte (Classical Latin lac, lactis, 'milk'). The Latin -ct- cluster regularly palatalised to -it in French (compare noctem -> nuit, factum -> fait).
lait.notes: Gives **le laitier** ('milkman, dairy') and **café au lait**.

laiton.etymology: From Old French laton / laiton ('brass, copper-zinc alloy'), attested across medieval Western Romance and Mediterranean trade (compare Arabic lāṭūn 'copper/brass'), reshaped in French under the influence of lait ('milk') because of the pale sheen of freshly polished brass.

cognates.meaning: medieval sheet brass (from Old French laton)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: laiton (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: laiton

lampe.etymology: Lampe comes via Late Latin lampada from Ancient Greek lampás, lampádos ('torch, oil lamp', from lámpein 'to shine').
lampe.notes: **Lampe de chevet** = bedside lamp; **lampe de poche** = pocket flashlight.

lanterne.etymology: Lanterne comes from Latin lanterna ('lantern, torch'), itself an early borrowing (via Etruscan) from Ancient Greek lamptḗr ('torch, lamp', from lámpein 'to shine').
lanterne.notes: Shares its ultimate Greek root 'to shine' with **la lampe**.

larme.etymology: Inherited via Old French lairme / larme from Classical Latin lacrima (archaic Old Latin dacrima), descending from the same Indo-European root as English tear.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: larme (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
