Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: larme

larme.notes: Colloquially in French cafés and kitchens, **une larme de lait / de miel** also means 'just a tiny drop' in a cup.

le.etymology: The article le and feminine la continue object-case forms of Latin demonstratives ille and illa. The direct-object pronouns le and la share that historical source, although articles and pronouns do different jobs today.

lentille.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin lenticula ('lentil'), diminutive of Classical Latin lens, lentis ('lentil'). In the seventeenth century, physicists named curved optical glass 'lentilles' (and English 'lenses' directly from Latin lens) because a biconvex glass disc is shaped just like a lentil seed.

cognates.meaning: from Old French lentille / directly from Latin lens

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: lentille (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: lentille

lentille.notes: In French, eyeglass lenses in frames are usually called **les verres de lunettes**, while contact lenses and camera lenses are **des lentilles**.

lettre.etymology: Lettre comes from Latin littera ('written character', and in the plural litterae 'epistle, written message'), evolving through Old French letre into both French lettre and English 'letter'.

libraire.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Classical Latin librarius ('copyist of manuscripts, bookseller'), derived from liber ('inner bark of a tree used for writing; book').

cognates.meaning: shifted in English to 'public/lending collection', whereas French librairie kept 'bookshop'

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: libraire (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: libraire

libraire.notes: Classic false friend: **un / une libraire** sells books in **une librairie** ('bookshop'), while a librarian in **une bibliothèque** is **un / une bibliothécaire**.

lierre.etymology: Formed in Middle French by agglutinating the elided definite article l' onto Old French ierre ('ivy'): l'ierre ('the ivy') was reanalyzed by speakers as a single noun le lierre! Old French ierre itself came regularly from Classical Latin hedera ('ivy').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: lierre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: lierre

lierre.notes: The same article fusion created French **le lendemain** ('the next day', from *l'endemain*) and **la luette** ('uvula', from *l'uette*).

lin.etymology: Inherited via Old French lin from Classical Latin linum ('flax plant, linen thread, linen cloth'), cognate with Ancient Greek línon.

cognates.meaning: lingerie comes from French linge (< lineus 'made of linen')

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: lin (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: lin

lin.notes: Normandy and northern France remain among the world's premier growers of flax (**le lin**), woven into tablecloths, bookbinding thread, and summer clothes.

lit.etymology: Lit descends regularly from Latin lectus ('couch, bed'): -ct- developed to -it and short e merged into i, producing Old French and modern French lit (with silent final t).
lit.notes: Gives **la literie** ('bedding'); **faire le lit** = to make the bed.

loquet.etymology: Diminutive formed in twelfth-century Old French from loc ('lock, bolt'), an early borrowing from Old English loc or Frankish/Old Norse lok ('fastener, bar, lock'). English latch and lock belong to the very same Germanic family.

cognates.meaning: lock; small hinged case (locket borrowed back from French loquet)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: loquet (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: loquet

lui.etymology: Lui continues Latin illi, a dative form of the demonstrative ille or illa. The Académie records ninth-century li. Modern lui can be an indirect-object form or a stressed pronoun.

lunettes.etymology: Lunette is the diminutive of lune ('moon', from Latin luna): a 'little moon' first meant a small round mirror or round glass lens in the Middle Ages, and in the plural **lunettes** came to mean a pair of eyeglasses.
lunettes.notes: Always plural for spectacles: **mes lunettes**, **une paire de lunettes**.

lutherie.etymology: Formed from luthier ('maker and repairer of stringed instruments'), derived from luth ('lute') < Old French leüt, borrowed via Old Occitan/Spanish from Arabic al-ʿūd ('the wood; the oud/lute').

cognates.meaning: all trace back to Arabic al-ʿūd

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: lutherie (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: lutherie

lutherie.notes: Even after violins eclipsed lutes in the 17th century, French kept **luthier** and **lutherie** for all bowed and plucked wooden instruments.

là.etymology: Là comes from Latin illac or illa, by that way or there. It is recorded in French from the eleventh century.

madame.etymology: Madame combines ma, my, and dame, lady. The Académie records this form of address from the twelfth century.

mais.etymology: Mais developed from Latin magis, more or rather. The French word is recorded from the tenth century; its history helps explain the move from preference or contrast to but.

manche.etymology: Feminine la manche ('sleeve') is inherited from Classical Latin manica ('long tunic sleeve reaching over the hand, handcuff'), derived from manus ('hand').

history.meaning: shirt or coat sleeve; narrow sea channel (la Manche)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: manche (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: manche

manche.notes: Masculine **le manche** ('broom or pan handle') comes from a closely related Latin derivative *manicus* ('part held in the hand').

manteau.etymology: Manteau comes from Latin mantellum ('cloak, cloth covering') via Old French mantel; vocalisation of final -el before plural -s produced manteau (compare English 'mantle' and 'mantelpiece').

mardi.etymology: Mardi continues Latin Martis dies, day of Mars. The twelfth-century French form marsdi preserves the older name more visibly.

marge.etymology: Adapted in Old and Middle French from Classical Latin margo, marginem ('edge, border, riverbank').

history.meaning: blank border of a page; leeway

cognates.meaning: borrowed via Old/Middle French or directly from Latin marginem

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: marge (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: marge

marge.notes: French school notebooks famously feature a red vertical line marking **la marge** on the left side of every squared page.

marmite.etymology: From Middle French marmite ('deep lidded cooking pot'), substantivized feminine of Old French adjective marmite ('demure, secretive, hiding one's face'), humorously applied to a covered pot that conceals what simmers inside.

cognates.meaning: named after the French earthenware cooking pot pictured on its label

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: marmite (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: marmite

marmite.notes: In French home cooking, **faire bouillir la marmite** ('keep the soup pot boiling') idiomatically means 'to keep the household fed and running'.

marteau.etymology: Inherited from Old French martel, from Late Latin martellus ('hammer'), diminutive of Imperial Latin martulus (an alteration of Classical Latin marculus 'small smith's hammer').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: marteau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: marteau

marteau.notes: Around 1709 Bartolomeo Cristofori invented the *gravicembalo col piano e forte* by replacing harpsichord plucks with tiny leather-and-felt **marteaux**.

menthe.etymology: Inherited via Old French mente from Classical Latin mentha ('mint'), borrowed from Ancient Greek mínthē (in myth, the nymph Minthe transformed into the fragrant herb).

cognates.meaning: early West Germanic borrowing from Latin mentha

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: menthe (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: menthe

menthe.notes: Hot green **thé à la menthe** steeped with fresh spearmint leaves is a beloved café staple across France.

menton.etymology: Inherited via Old French menton from Vulgar Latin *mentonem, enlarged from Classical Latin mentum ('chin', from an Indo-European root *men- 'to jut out', also seen in promontoire and éminent).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: menton (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: menton

menton.notes: Watch out for the look-alike verb **mentir** ('to tell a lie', from Latin *mentiri* 'to fabricate in the mind' < *mens*) — completely unrelated to **le menton**!

merci.etymology: Merci comes from Latin merces, which meant pay or a price and later favour or grace. The Académie records ninth-century mercit with the sense of grace or mercy. Modern merci is the everyday expression of thanks; the older sense survives in sans merci.

history.meaning: pay, price; later favour or grace

merci.notes:
- Answer to *merci* is usually *de rien* or *je vous en prie*.
- *Non, merci* declines an offer; *Oui, merci* accepts it.

meuble.etymology: Shortened from biens meubles ('movable goods'), inherited from Spoken Latin *movibilis (Classical Latin mobilis, 'movable', from movere 'to move'). In medieval law property was either immeuble ('immovable': land and buildings) or meuble ('movable': chests, tables, beds).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: meuble (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: meuble

midi.etymology: Midi combines the older French elements mi, middle, and di, day. They descend from Latin medius and dies. The combination originally identifies the middle of the day.

miel.etymology: Miel comes directly from Latin mel ('honey'), with regular diphthongisation of stressed short e into ie (as in caelum -> ciel).

miette.etymology: Double diminutive formed in Old French from mie ('soft inner crumb of bread, tiny bit') + -ette, inherited from Classical Latin mica ('crumb, grain of salt, tiny morsel').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: miette (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: miette

miette.notes: Modern French still distinguishes **la croûte** ('crust'), **la mie** ('soft inside of the loaf'), and **les miettes** ('loose crumbs').

mijoter.etymology: Attested from Middle/Classical French in regional northern usage (originally 'to coddle, store fruit gently in straw or crumbs to ripen', then 'to cook very slowly over low heat'), expressive derivative built on Old French mie / Picard mijot.

history.meaning: to simmer slowly over gentle heat

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: mijoter (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: mijoter

mijoter.notes: Figuratively, **Qu'est-ce que vous mijotez?** means 'What scheme or surprise are you cooking up?'.

mille.etymology: The number mille was borrowed from Latin mille, thousand. Its French history is recorded from the eleventh century; the number does not take an ordinary plural s.

minuit.etymology: Compound inherited from Old French mienuit ('the middle of the night'), combining feminine mie (< Latin media 'middle') and nuit (< Latin noctem 'night'), exactly parallel to midi (< medius dies 'midday').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: minuit (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: minuit

minuit.notes: Originally feminine because *nuit* is feminine, **minuit** shifted to masculine on the model of **midi**.

minute.etymology: The time word minute comes from medieval Latin minuta, a noun use of the feminine of minutus, small. The Académie records it from the thirteenth century. The separate document-draft sense has its own specialised history.

miroir.etymology: Miroir comes from Old French mireor, built on mirer ('to look at, gaze at', from Latin mirari 'to wonder at, admire'). English 'mirror' was borrowed directly from Old French.
miroir.notes: **Regarder dans le miroir** = to look in the mirror.

moi.etymology: Moi continues Latin me, me. The Académie records ninth-century French mi. It is the stressed object form rather than the subject form je.

moineau.etymology: Diminutive in -eau (Old French moignel) of moine ('monk' < Late Latin monachus), affectionately naming the house sparrow after the brown-and-grey hood of its plumage, which reminded medieval observers of a friar's cowl.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: moineau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: moineau

moineau.notes: Older French called a sparrow **un passereau** (from Latin *passer*), which survives in **les passereaux** ('songbirds'), while cheeky little **moineau** ('little monk') won everyday speech!

mon.etymology: Mon and its feminine counterpart ma descend from Latin meus, mea and meum. The Académie records tenth-century mo. Modern forms agree with the possessed noun rather than naming the owner’s gender.

monde.etymology: Monde, world, descends from Latin mundus with the same meaning. It is recorded from the twelfth century. The rare adjective monde, clean, is a different dictionary entry.

monter.etymology: Monter comes from later Latin montare, to go up, derived from mons or montis, mountain. The French verb is recorded from the tenth century; riding and mounting are related extensions.

montre.etymology: Montre is a noun built from montrer ('to show, display', from Latin monstrare). It first named a shop display case and the visible dial that 'showed' the hours, before naming a pocket watch or wristwatch.

mortier.etymology: Inherited via Old French mortier from Classical Latin mortarium ('stone or wooden trough in which lime and sand — or kitchen herbs — are pounded together; the mortar mixed in it').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French mortier and Latin mortarium

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: mortier (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: mortier

mortier.notes: Just as in English, **un mortier** means both the mason's lime-and-sand mix between flagstones and the kitchen mortar used with a pestle (**un pilon**).

motus.etymology: Playful 17th-century mock-Latin interjection built on French mot ('word' < Late Latin muttum 'muttered sound') + humorous Latinate ending -us, popularized in classical comedy for '(not a) word! hush!'.

history.meaning: not a word! mum's the word!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: motus (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: motus

motus.notes: Because of its mock-Latin disguise, the final *-s* of **motus** **/mɔtys/** is always pronounced aloud, especially in the beloved idiom **Motus et bouche cousue!** ('Mum's the word and lips sealed!').

muet.etymology: Old French diminutive built on mu ('mute, silent', from Latin mutus) + -et. As one-syllable mu risked homophony in speech, the fuller form muet replaced it completely by Middle French.

cognates.meaning: silent (from Latin mutus / Old French muet)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: muet (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: muet

mystère.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French from Latin mysterium, from Ancient Greek mystḗrion ('secret rite, hidden truth'), derived from mýstēs ('initiate') and mýein ('to close the eyes or lips').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: mystère (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: mystère

mystère.notes: Note the medieval homograph: Old French *mestier* ('craft, guild', modern **métier**, from Latin *ministerium*) was sometimes spelled *mystère* when craft guilds staged medieval 'mystery plays'!

mélodie.etymology: Learned borrowing via Late Latin melodia from Ancient Greek melōidía ('singing, choral song, tune'), compounded from mélos ('limb; musical phrase') and ōidḗ ('song', source of ode).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: mélodie (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: mélodie

nappe.etymology: Nappe comes from Latin mappa ('napkin, signal cloth'), with dissimilation of initial m- to n- before -pp- in Popular Latin *nappa. English 'napkin' and 'apron' (originally 'a napron') both come from this French word!
nappe.notes: False friend: **la nappe** is a tablecloth; a napkin is **une serviette**.

ne.etymology: The negative ne continues Latin non. Its French history is recorded from the tenth century. The chemical abbreviation Ne belongs to an unrelated Greek-derived name.

non.etymology: Non continues Latin non. The Académie analyses the older Latin expression as *ne oinum, not a single one; the asterisk marks a reconstructed earlier form.

notre.etymology: Notre comes from Latin noster, our. Ninth-century French had nostro. Modern plural nos belongs to this same possessive series.

nous.etymology: Nous descends from Latin nos, meaning we or us. The Académie dates the French pronoun to the ninth century. Modern nous still has both subject and object uses, so its history fits a wider range than the single English gloss we.

nouveau.etymology: Nouveau descends from Latin novellus, young or recent, itself related to novus, new. Twelfth-century French had novel; the alternative nouvel preserves that older shape.

nouvelle.etymology: The noun nouvelle, news, comes from Latin novella, a noun use of the neuter plural of novellus, new or recent. Its plural use for news should be distinguished from the adjective nouvelle and from the later literary sense short story.

noyer.etymology: Inherited from Spoken Latin *nucarius ('walnut tree'), derived from Classical Latin nux, nucis ('nut, walnut'—which itself gave French noix). Like chêne or merisier, the tree name also names its timber.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: noyer (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: noyer

noyer.notes: An accidental homograph of the verb **noyer** ('to drown', from Latin *necare*), which has a completely separate origin.

nuit.etymology: Nuit continues Latin nox, with the stem noct-. The Académie records tenth-century noit before the modern spelling.

oh.etymology: Oh is an expressive interjection recorded in French from the sixteenth century. The Académie considers borrowing from the same Latin exclamation probable, rather than presenting that route as certain.

oignon.etymology: Inherited from Old French oignon, from Classical Latin unionem (accusative of unio, 'oneness, single large pearl; country Latin word for a single-bulb onion', contrasted with multi-clove garlic).

cognates.meaning: onion was borrowed from Old French oignon; union is its learned Latin doublet!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: oignon (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: oignon

oignon.notes: Old French wrote *oign-* to represent palatal /ɲ/ after *o*; the 1990 spelling reform also permits **ognon** to match modern pronunciation /ɔɲɔ̃/.

ombre.etymology: Inherited directly from Classical Latin umbra ('shadow, shade'), with regular Romance lowering of short Latin u to /o/ nasalised before m + consonant.

cognates.meaning: little shade (via Italian ombrello from Latin umbra)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: ombre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: ombre

on.etymology: On descends from Latin homo, meaning a human being. The Académie records om in the ninth century and hom or hum in the eleventh. A noun referring to a person became a subject pronoun; its older noun-like construction also explains l’on.
on.notes: The possessive can depend on the meaning: general on can go with son/sa/ses; when on means nous, notre/nos is common.

orage.etymology: Inherited from Old French orage (originally 'strong wind, gust of air'), from Vulgar Latin *auraticum, built on Classical Latin aura ('breeze, breath of air', borrowed from Greek aúra).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: orage (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: orage

orage.notes: Unrelated to *or* ('gold')—its initial *or-* reflects Latin *au-* (*aura* -> *or-*), just as *aurum* gave *or*.

oreille.etymology: Inherited from Classical/Colloquial Latin auricula ('earlobe, little ear'), diminutive of Classical Latin auris ('ear'). Across all Romance languages, spoken Latin preferred the expressive diminutive auricula over short auris.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: oreille (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: oreille

oreille.notes: Adding *-er* to *oreille* produced **un oreiller**—literally 'the thing for your ear', i.e. a pillow!

orteil.etymology: Inherited from Old French arteil ('toe'), from Classical Latin articulus ('little joint, knuckle, digit'), whose initial vowel shifted from a- to o- in Gallo-Romance through the influence of Gaulish ordiga ('big toe').

cognates.meaning: learned doublet of orteil from Latin articulus

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: orteil (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: orteil

orteil.notes: Few pairs look more surprising than **un orteil** ('a toe') and **un article** ('a newspaper article'), yet both trace back to Latin *articulus*!

oui.etymology: Oui developed from Old French oïl, an affirmative response. The Académie dates the modern form to the fourteenth century.

ouvert.etymology: Ouvert is the past participle and adjective of ouvrir ('to open'), descending from Vulgar Latin *opertus (for Classical Latin apertus 'open, uncovered').
ouvert.notes: Feminine **ouverte** sounds the final t (/uvɛʁt/). English 'overt' was borrowed from Old French.

ouvrir.etymology: Ouvrir descends from Vulgar Latin *operire (a blend of Classical Latin aperire 'to open' with cooperire 'to cover', which gave couvrir). Intervocalic -p- voiced and softened to -v-.
ouvrir.notes: Conjugates like a -er verb in the singular present (*j'ouvre, tu ouvres, il ouvre*) despite its -ir infinitive; past participle **ouvert**.

où.etymology: Où descends from Latin ubi, where. The Académie records the French question word from the tenth century.

pain.etymology: Pain descends from Latin panis ('bread, loaf'). From Old French onward it has stood at the centre of daily meals and expressions such as gagner son pain ('to earn one's living') and copain (literally 'one who shares bread').

panier.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin panarium ('breadbasket'), derived from panis ('bread', French pain) + -arium. Long after baskets came to carry everything at market, the word still preserves 'bread' at its core.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: panier (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: panier

papier.etymology: Papier comes via Latin papyrus from Ancient Greek pápyros ('Nile papyrus sedge, writing sheet'), shifting in the late Middle Ages to rag-and-pulp paper.

parler.etymology: Parler continues Christian Latin parabolare, to speak, related to parabola, speech. That word was borrowed from Greek parabolê, comparison or parable. The French verb is recorded from the tenth century.

partition.etymology: From Latin partitio ('division into parts', from partiri 'to divide'). In seventeenth-century music (matching Italian partitura), une partition meant dividing an ensemble piece onto aligned staves on one page so every voice or hand could be read together—hence 'musical score / sheet music'.

history.meaning: musical score arranged in aligned staves

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: partition (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: partition

pas.etymology: The negative pas began as the noun for a step, from Latin passus. It first strengthened negatives with movement verbs by referring to even a tiny distance, then became a general spoken negative marker.

passer.etymology: Passer comes from a reconstructed later Latin *passare, derived from passus, step. The Académie records the French verb from the eleventh century.

patrimoine.etymology: Borrowed in Old French from Classical Latin patrimonium ('inheritance passed down from a father', from pater, patris 'father'). Expanded in modern French from family estate to shared cultural and architectural heritage (le patrimoine historique).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: patrimoine (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: patrimoine

paume.etymology: Inherited from Old French paume, from Classical Latin palma ('palm of the hand; palm tree frond whose spread leaves resemble an open hand'), with regular vocalization of Latin -l- before -m-.

history.meaning: palm of the hand; palm branch

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French paume / Latin palma

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: paume (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: paume

paume.notes: Striking a ball with the bare **paume** gave medieval France **le jeu de paume** ('real/court tennis'), the direct ancestor of modern tennis.

perdre.etymology: Perdre descends from Latin perdere, originally to give wastefully and later to destroy or ruin. The Académie records the French verb from the ninth century.

persil.etymology: Inherited via Old French perresil / persil from Late Latin petrosilinum, borrowed from Ancient Greek petrosélinon ('rock celery', compound of pétra 'rock' + sélinon 'celery, parsley').

cognates.meaning: blended from Old English petersilie and Old French perresil

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: persil (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: persil

persil.notes: Greek **sélinon** in the second half of **persil** is also the exact source of French **céleri** ('celery')!

petit.etymology: Petit is traced to a Gallo-Romance form *pit- expressing smallness. Medieval Latin pititus provides evidence for that family; the reconstructed base is marked with an asterisk.

peu.etymology: Peu continues Latin paucum, few or little. Early French spellings included pou, poi and po before peu became established.

peut-être.etymology: Peut-être joins peut, the he/she present form of pouvoir, and être, to be. Twelfth-century expressions included put cel estre and puet estre; the hyphenated form is recorded in the seventeenth century.

pharmacien.etymology: Formed in Classical French from pharmacie ('apothecary art, pharmacy'), via Medieval Latin pharmacia from Ancient Greek pharmakeía ('preparation of remedies'), from phármakon ('medicinal herb, remedy').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: pharmacien (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: pharmacien

pharmacien.notes: In 1777, a royal declaration in France officially established the *Collège de pharmacie*, replacing the older guild title **apothicaire** with **pharmacien**.

pierre.etymology: Pierre comes from Latin petra ('rock, stone', borrowed from Ancient Greek pétra). Diphthongisation of open e to ie and lenition of -tr- to -rr- yielded Old French piere, pierre.
pierre.notes: Also the source of the first name *Pierre* ('Peter'); **en pierre** = made of stone.

pinceau.etymology: Inherited from Old French pincel, from Vulgar Latin *penicellus, a variant of Classical Latin penicillus ('painter's fine brush', originally 'little tuft of tail hair', double diminutive of penis 'tail').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French pincel (originally a fine camel-hair brush before graphite!)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: pinceau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: pinceau

pinceau.notes: Watch the false friend: English *pencil* came from Old French *pincel*, but in modern French **un pinceau** is a paintbrush and **un crayon** is a pencil (and **penicillin** was named in Latin for its brush-shaped mold!).

piste.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (originally in horsemanship) from Italian pista ('beaten track left by hooves, trail'), feminine participial noun of Late Latin pistare ('to pound, tread down', frequentative of pinsere).

history.meaning: trail, clue track, ski run, bike lane

cognates.meaning: pounded basil sauce (from the same Late Latin pistare!)
ski run or fencing strip, borrowed from French

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: piste (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: piste

piste.notes: **Une piste** ('trodden trail') and Italian **pesto** ('pounded sauce') come from the very same verb meaning 'to pound or tread down'!

pièce.etymology: Pièce is traced to reconstructed Gaulish *pettia, a small piece. Its French history is recorded from the eleventh century. The theatre sense is one of several later uses of this general noun.

place.etymology: Place came through Latin platea from Greek plateia hodos, a broad street. The French noun is recorded from the eleventh century; its modern senses include a location, space or seat.

plafond.etymology: Originally spelled plat-fonds or plat fond in sixteenth-century architecture—literally 'flat bottom / flat underside' (plat 'flat' + fond 'bottom, background'), describing a flat boarded or plastered ceiling underside as opposed to an open arched vault. Fused into plafond in the seventeenth century.

history.meaning: flat underside of an upper floor

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: plafond (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: plafond

plaire.etymology: Plaire is a remodelling of the older French verb plaisir, itself descended from Latin placere, to be pleasing. The Académie dates plaire to the twelfth century.

plan.etymology: Plan blends two related Latin origins: planus ('flat, level surface', giving a flat architectural drawing or town map) and plantare ('to lay out on the ground'), expanding from a floor plan to any project or scheme.
plan.notes: **Un plan de la ville** = a city map; **un bon plan** = a good idea/deal.

pluie.etymology: Pluie comes from Popular Latin *ploia (for Classical Latin pluvia, 'rain', from pluere 'to rain'), matching Italian pioggia.
pluie.notes: Paired with the impersonal verb **pleuvoir** (*il pleut* = 'it is raining').

poids.etymology: Inherited from Old French peis / pois ('weight'), from Vulgar Latin pensum ('amount weighed out', neuter participle of pendere 'to hang on a scale, weigh'). Sixteenth-century humanists inserted a silent -d- in poids on the mistaken belief that it came from Latin pondus!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: poids (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: poids

poids.notes: From the same Latin *pensare* ('to weigh carefully') come both **peser** ('to weigh') and **penser** ('to think—to weigh in the mind')!

point.etymology: Point descends from Latin punctum, a prick, tiny hole or dot, related to pungere, to prick. The Académie dates the noun to the eleventh century. Expressions such as au point extend the noun’s range.

pomme.etymology: Pomme comes from Late Latin poma (originally the neuter plural of Classical Latin pomum 'tree fruit', reinterpreted as a feminine singular). In French it narrowed specifically to the apple.

poncer.etymology: Derived from ponce ('pumice', in pierre ponce 'pumice stone', inherited from Latin pumicem). Before modern sandpaper, cabinetmakers smoothed wood and parchment by rubbing them with powdered pumice stone.

history.meaning: pumice -> to polish or smooth with pumice, then sandpaper

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: poncer (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: poncer

pont.etymology: Pont comes directly from Latin pons, pontis ('bridge'). Its accusative pontem regularly yielded Old French and modern French pont.
pont.notes: In French work life, **faire le pont** means taking a Friday or Monday off between a holiday and the weekend.

porcelaine.etymology: Borrowed via Italian porcellana (attested in Marco Polo's travels). In Italian porcellana first meant the smooth, glossy white cowrie shell (diminutive of porcella 'little sow', from a perceived shell shape); Europeans transferred the shell's name to translucent white Chinese ceramic with the same pearly lustre.

history.meaning: glossy white cowrie shell -> fine Chinese ceramic

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: porcelaine (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: porcelaine

porche.etymology: Inherited from Old French porche, from Classical Latin porticus ('colonnaded gallery, covered entrance porch'), derived from porta ('gate, entranceway').

cognates.meaning: porch was borrowed directly from Old French porche
learned doublet portique + base noun porte

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: porche (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: porche

porche.notes: In French towns, **un porche** often names the deep vaulted stone carriageway leading from the street into a quiet inner courtyard (**la cour**).

porte.etymology: Porte comes directly from Latin porta ('city gate, doorway'), sharing an Indo-European root for crossing or passing through with port ('harbour') and porter ('to carry').
porte.notes: Compare **le portail** ('large courtyard or driveway gate') from the same Latin family.

portrait.etymology: Substantivized past participle of Old and Middle French portraire ('to draw forth, trace line by line, depict'), inherited from Classical Latin protrahere ('to draw forward, bring to light': pro- + trahere 'to draw').

history.meaning: to draw, depict -> drawn image, likeness

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old/Middle French portraire and portrait
drawn stroke or facial feature (from simple Latin trahere, tractum)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: portrait (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: portrait

portrait.notes: Notice how **portrait** and **trait** share Latin *trahere* ('to draw a line'): hence the French idiom **tout le portrait de... / trait pour trait** ('the spitting image of...').

poser.etymology: Poser comes curiously from Late Latin pausare ('to pause, rest', from Greek paûsis 'cessation'), which in Romance took over the meanings of Classical Latin ponere ('to put, place') because of their similar past participles.
poser.notes: **Poser une valise** = to set down a suitcase; **poser une question** = to ask a question.

poterie.etymology: Formed in twelfth-century Old French from potier ('potter', itself from pot + -ier) plus the craft/collective suffix -ie. English pottery was borrowed directly from Old French poterie.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: poterie (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: poterie

pouce.etymology: Inherited via Old French polce from Classical Latin pollex, pollicem ('thumb, big toe').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: pouce (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: pouce

pouce.notes: Giving someone a gentle nudge forward with your thumb inspired **donner un coup de pouce** ('to lend a helping hand'), while playground truces cry **Pouce!** ('Time-out!').

poudre.etymology: Inherited via Old French polre -> poldre -> poudre (with regular glide consonant -d- inserted between -l- and -r-, followed by vocalization of -l- to -u-) from Classical Latin pulvis, pulverem ('dust, fine powder').

cognates.meaning: powder was borrowed directly from Old French poudre

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: poudre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: poudre

poudre.notes: In French baking, **sucre en poudre** is granulated/caster sugar (not icing sugar, which is **sucre glace**!), and **poudre d'amandes** is ground almonds.

pour.etymology: Pour continues Latin pro. The Académie records French pro in the ninth century, por and pur in the eleventh, and pour in the thirteenth.

pouvoir.etymology: Pouvoir descends from reconstructed Popular Latin *potere, a remodelling of Classical Latin posse, to be able. Earlier French forms included poeir before pouvoir became established.

prendre.etymology: Prendre comes from Latin prendere, a contracted form of prehendere, meaning to grasp or take. The Académie dates the French verb to the ninth century. The idea of taking underlies its many extended senses.
prendre.notes: Very common: *prendre le petit-déjeuner*, *prendre une décision*, *prendre un bain*. Note the stem change: *il prend* but *ils prennent*.

presque.etymology: Presque developed from combinations involving the older French pres and que. The Académie records stages such as bien pres que and pres que before the words became the modern adverb.

printemps.etymology: Inherited from Spoken Latin *primum tempus ('first season, start of the fine weather', from primus 'first' + tempus 'time, season'), replacing Classical Latin ver. Fused in Old French as printens, later respelled printemps after temps.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: printemps (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: printemps

problème.etymology: Problème was borrowed through Latin problema from Greek problêma, something put forward and then a task or question. The French noun is recorded from the fourteenth century.

prochain.etymology: Prochain descends from reconstructed later Latin *propeanus, derived from prope, near. The French adjective is recorded from the twelfth century; its history connects next with nearness.

promenade.etymology: Formed in the 16th century with suffix -ade from promener ('to take for a walk, walk back and forth'), earlier Old French pormener (por- 'forth' + mener 'to lead' < Late Latin minare 'to drive/lead onward').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: promenade (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: promenade

promenade.notes: **Une promenade** names both the act of strolling (**faire une promenade**) and the scenic tree-lined avenue itself.

proposer.etymology: Proposer was borrowed from Latin proponere, to place before someone or set forth. Its French shape was influenced by poser. The Académie records it from the twelfth century.

propriétaire.etymology: Propriétaire comes from Late Latin proprietarius ('owner of property', from proprietas 'ownership', built on proprius 'one's own').
propriétaire.notes: Same form for masculine and feminine (**le / la propriétaire**).

pupitre.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (pupiltre -> pupitre) from Classical Latin pulpitum ('wooden platform, reading stand, lectern'—the same Latin word that gave English pulpit).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: pupitre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: pupitre

pénible.etymology: Pénible is derived from peine, trouble or effort. The Académie dates the adjective to the twelfth century. It is not explained by simply assigning a generic meaning to the ending -ible.

pétrir.etymology: Inherited from Old French pestrir ('to knead dough'), from Late/Vulgar Latin *pisturire, built on Classical Latin pistura ('pounding grain, baking') and pistor ('baker', originally 'grain-pounder', from pinsere 'to crush, knead').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: pétrir (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: pétrir

pétrir.notes: The wooden kneading trough in a traditional French bakery is called **le pétrin** (whence the idiom *être dans le pétrin*, 'to be in a sticky jam').

qu'est-ce.etymology: Qu'est-ce contracts que ('what', from Latin quid) + est ('is', from Latin est) + ce ('that/it', from Latin ecce hoc), forming the standard spoken French opening for 'what' questions (*qu'est-ce qui*, *qu'est-ce que*).
qu'est-ce.notes: Pronounced /kɛs/ as a single smooth syllable before *qui* or *que*.

qu'est-ce que.etymology: This question expression combines interrogative que, the verb est and the demonstrative ce, followed by que. The Académie treats the interrogative construction under que. Its pieces became a familiar way to introduce a question about an object.

quand.etymology: Quand continues Latin quando, when. The Académie records the French word from the eleventh century.

quatorze.etymology: Quatorze descends from Latin quattuordecim, built from the words for four and ten. It is recorded in French from the twelfth century.

que.etymology: Several older words converged in French que. Interrogative que continues Latin quid; relative que continues quem; the connecting conjunction developed from quia. These histories help explain why one spelling has different grammatical jobs.

quel.etymology: Quel descends from Latin qualis, of what kind or nature. The Académie records the French word from the tenth century.

quelqu'un.etymology: Quelqu’un combines the indefinite quelque and un. The Académie records the compound from the thirteenth century. The apostrophe marks the joining of these two pieces.

quelque.etymology: Quelque was formed from quel and the conjunction que. The Académie records the combination from the eleventh century.

qui.etymology: Relative qui continues Latin qui, while interrogative qui continues Latin quis. The Académie records the relative in the ninth century and the question word in the tenth; their modern spellings coincide.

quoi.etymology: Quoi is the stressed descendant of Latin quid ('what?'), where Latin short i opened to e and diphthongised in stressed position through ei and oi to /kwa/.
quoi.notes: Used after prepositions (*avec quoi?*, *de quoi?*) or at the end of spoken questions (*C'était quoi?*).

raccourci.etymology: Substantivized past participle (16th–17th century) of raccourcir ('to shorten': re- + accourcir, built on court 'short' < Classical Latin curtus).

cognates.meaning: from Latin curtus and Middle French courtault

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: raccourci (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: raccourci

raccourci.notes: Today **un raccourci** means both a cobbled alley shortcut (**prendre un raccourci**) and a keyboard shortcut (**un raccourci clavier**).

rappeler.etymology: Rappeler is a French derivative of appeler. The Académie records it from the eleventh century. The additional beginning can contribute the sense of calling again or calling back.

rebours.etymology: From Old French rebors ('bristling the wrong way, contrary'), inherited from Late Latin reburrus ('with hair standing up backward', from re- 'back' + burra 'shaggy wool, coarse nap'). Brushing cloth or fur à rebours meant stroking it against the grain—hence 'in reverse' and un compte à rebours ('countdown').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: rebours (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: rebours

recette.etymology: Inherited via Old French receite ('money or goods received; medical/culinary formula') from Medieval Latin recepta, substantivized feminine/neuter plural of Classical Latin receptus (from recipere 'to receive, take'), echoing the apothecary heading Recipe ('Take...').

history.meaning: to take, receive -> things received; formula

cognates.meaning: receipt came from Anglo-Norman receite (note old cookbooks called recipes 'receipts'!)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: recette (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: recette

recette.notes: **Une recette** still keeps both historical meanings in French: **une recette de cuisine** ('a recipe') and **les recettes** ('box-office or shop takings').

regarder.etymology: Regarder was formed in Old French from re- + garder ('to watch, guard', from Frankish *wardon 'to keep watch', cognate with English 'ward' and 'regard').
regarder.notes: No preposition for 'at': **regarder l'étiquette** = 'to look at the label'.

registre.etymology: Inherited from Old French registre, from Medieval Latin registrum, an alteration of Late Latin regesta ('matters recorded or entered in a book', neuter plural past participle of regerere 'to carry back, transcribe').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: registre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: registre

registre.notes: From organ stops (**tirer les registres**), **le registre** also entered music and linguistics to mean vocal range or tone of speech (`tu` vs `vous`).

rendez-vous.etymology: Rendez-vous began as an instruction: the polite or plural imperative of se rendre. The Académie records the expression used as a noun from the sixteenth century.

retard.etymology: Retard is a noun formed from retarder, to delay. The Académie dates the noun to the seventeenth century. The modern expression en retard means late.

revoir.etymology: Revoir is derived from voir, to see, with the idea of seeing again. The Académie records tenth-century revedeir and twelfth-century reveoir.

rien.etymology: Rien descends from Latin rem, the object-case form of res, thing. The French word is recorded from the tenth century; negative constructions gave this older thing-word its familiar modern meaning nothing.

ronronner.etymology: Nineteenth-century French verb built on the reduplicated onomatopoeia ronron ('a cat's purr'), imitating a steady low vibration.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: ronronner (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: ronronner

ruban.etymology: Attested in thirteenth-century Old French as riban / ruban, likely borrowed from Middle Dutch ringhband ('neckband, collar ribbon'). Middle English riban—modern English ribbon—came straight from the Old Northern French form.

cognates.meaning: narrow woven strip (from Old French riban)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: ruban (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: ruban

rue.etymology: Rue comes from Late Latin ruga ('wrinkle, furrow', and by extension a 'wheel-rutted path' or 'lined street between houses'), developing into Old French rue ('town street').
rue.notes: Diminutive **une ruelle** = a narrow alley or side lane.

réserver.etymology: Réserver was borrowed from Latin reservare, to put aside or keep. The Académie records the French verb from the twelfth century.

réunion.etymology: Réunion is derived from réunir. Its fifteenth-century senses included reconciliation or agreement before the broader idea of bringing together and the modern meeting sense.

réveiller.etymology: Réveiller is derived from éveiller, to wake. The Académie records the derivative from the twelfth century. The reflexive se réveiller describes waking up oneself.

rêve.etymology: Rêve is a noun formed from rêver. The Académie records the noun from the seventeenth century; this account does not claim a settled deeper origin for rêver.

s'asseoir.etymology: Asseoir descends from Vulgar Latin *assedere (Classical Latin assidere, ad + sedere 'to sit beside'). Reflexive **s'asseoir** means 'to sit down'.

sac.etymology: Sac comes from Latin saccus ('bag, sack'), borrowed via Ancient Greek sákkos from Semitic *śaq ('coarse cloth, sack').
sac.notes: **Sac à main** = handbag; **sac à dos** = backpack.

salle.etymology: Salle came through Latin sala from reconstructed Old Low Franconian *sal, a dwelling consisting of a single room. The French word is recorded from the eleventh century.

salut.etymology: Salut descends from Latin salus, physical well-being or health, related to salvus, safe or well. Wishing someone good health helped the word develop its greeting sense.

sauver.etymology: Sauver comes from Late Latin salvare ('to save, preserve', built on Classical Latin salvus 'safe, unharmed'). Vocalisation of l before v turned salvare into Old French salver, sauver.
sauver.notes: Related to **sauf** ('safe' in *sain et sauf*, and preposition 'except').

savoir.etymology: Savoir continues Latin sapere. That verb could refer both to taste or smell and to discernment or wisdom. The Académie dates French savoir to the ninth century: the history connects sensory judgement with knowing.
savoir.notes:
- *Savoir* is for facts and learned skills; *connaître* is for people, places and being familiar with something.
- *Je ne sais pas* is often shortened in speech to *chais pas*.

sceau.etymology: Inherited via Old French seel ('signet ring, stamped wax emblem') from Classical Latin sigillum ('little figure, seal impression'), diminutive of signum ('mark, sign'); spelled sceau with etymological sc- from the Renaissance.

cognates.meaning: seal was borrowed from Old French seel!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: sceau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: sceau

sceau.notes: Famous French homophone quartet **/so/**: **un sceau** ('a wax seal'), **un seau** ('a bucket'), **un saut** ('a jump'), and **sot** ('foolish')!

se.etymology: Se continues Latin se, oneself. It is recorded in French from the ninth century. Its modern reflexive uses belong to that pronoun history, not to the chemical abbreviation Se.

seau.etymology: Inherited via Old French seel from Vulgar Latin *sitellum, masculine diminutive of Classical Latin situla ('well bucket, pail').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: seau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: seau

seau.notes: Famous French homophone trio all pronounced `/so/`: **un seau** ('a bucket'), **un sceau** ('a wax seal', < *sigillum*), and **un saut** ('a jump', < *saltum*).

sel.etymology: Inherited directly from Classical Latin sal ('salt'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *séh₂ls, one of the oldest and best-preserved culinary words across European languages.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: sel (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: sel

sel.notes: Latin *sal* also gave French **la salade** ('salted greens'), **la sauce** (*salsa* 'salted dressing'), and **le salaire** (*salarium*).

semaine.etymology: Semaine descends from Christian Latin septimana, related to an adjective meaning concerning the number seven. The French word is recorded from the eleventh century.

serviette.etymology: Serviette was formed in Middle French from servir ('to serve at table', from Latin servire) + diminutive -ette: originally the cloth used when serving at table, and later also a bath towel or briefcase.
serviette.notes: Context tells you whether **une serviette** is a napkin at breakfast or a towel in a hotel bathroom.

seul.etymology: Seul continues Latin solus, alone or only. The Académie records the French adjective from the tenth century.

si.etymology: The conditional si continues Latin si, if. The affirmative reply si has a different source, Latin sic, thus or yes. The musical note with the same spelling has a separate history.

signer.etymology: Signer was remodelled after signe from older French seigner, which came from Latin signare, to mark or seal. The Académie distinguishes the thirteenth-century sense make a sign from the sixteenth-century signature sense.

soie.etymology: Inherited via Old French seie / soie from Classical Latin saeta ('coarse animal hair, bristle'), which in Late Latin phrases like seta serica ('Seric/Chinese strand') shifted to mean 'silk thread, silk fabric'.

cognates.meaning: borrowed via French from Arabic zaytūnī

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: soie (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: soie

soie.notes: Notice **le papier de soie**: in French, crisp ultra-thin wrapping tissue paper is poetically called 'silk paper'.

soir.etymology: Soir descends from Latin serus, late or of the evening. The Académie records tenth-century ser before the twelfth-century form soir.

soirée.etymology: Soirée is derived from soir. It is recorded from the thirteenth century and can refer to the evening as a period spent doing something, or to an evening event.

son.etymology: The possessive son, with feminine sa, continues Latin suus, sua and suum. The Académie dates it to the ninth century. It is historically separate from the nouns son meaning sound or bran.

sonner.etymology: Sonner comes from Latin sonare ('to sound, ring, resound', from sonus 'sound'). It covers both ringing a bell and a clock striking the hour.
sonner.notes: Gives **la sonnette** ('bell, buzzer') and **la sonnerie** ('ringtone, chime').

souci.etymology: Souci derives from Old French soucier ('to trouble, worry', from Latin sollicitare 'to disturb, make anxious').
souci.notes: **Pas de souci!** = No worries! / No problem!

soucoupe.etymology: Formed from sous ('under') + coupe ('cup, goblet', or modelled on Italian sottocoppa). Originally a small footed salver held underneath a goblet when serving wine at table; with the arrival of tea, coffee, and chocolate in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, it became the modern saucer.

history.meaning: tray held beneath a drinking goblet
porcelain or earthenware saucer under a teacup

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: soucoupe (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: soucoupe

soulever.etymology: Soulever comes from Old French souzlever (sous 'under' + lever 'to raise', from Latin sublevare): literally 'to lift from underneath'.

soupe.etymology: Soupe comes from Late Latin suppa (of Germanic origin, related to English 'sop' and 'sup'), originally meaning the slice of bread placed in a bowl over which hot broth was poured, and later the soup itself.
soupe.notes: **Un bol de soupe chaude** = a bowl of hot soup.

stressé.etymology: Stressé is the past participle of stresser used as an adjective. Stresser is a twentieth-century derivative of stress; it is not an adjective whose origin can be inferred from the last letters alone.

stylo.etymology: Stylo is a twentieth-century shortening of stylographe. The shortened form became the ordinary French word for a pen.

sucre.etymology: Sucre entered Old French via Medieval Latin succarum and Italian zucchero from Arabic sukkar, which traced back through Persian šakar to Sanskrit śárkarā ('gravel, grit, crystal sugar').

super.etymology: Informal super is a twentieth-century use derived from the super- word family. The Académie distinguishes this favourable adjective or exclamation from the noun for a type of fuel.

sur.etymology: Sur continues Latin super, on or above. The French preposition is recorded from the ninth century. It is separate from the accented adjective sûr.

sûr.etymology: Sûr descends from Latin securus, free from concern or safe. The Académie records it from the eleventh century. The written accent distinguishes it from the unrelated preposition sur.

table.etymology: Table comes from Latin tabula ('board, plank, writing tablet, table'), passing through Old French table into both modern French and English.
table.notes: **À table!** = Dinner/breakfast is ready!; **tablette** ('shelf; digital tablet') is its diminutive.

tablier.etymology: Inherited from Old French tablier (originally 'tablecloth', 'board for table games', and by the 15th century 'protective cloth worn in front at a workbench or kitchen table'), derived from table (< Latin tabula 'board, table').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: tablier (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tablier

tablier.notes: In civil engineering, **le tablier d'un pont** still preserves the older 'flat planked board' sense: it means the deck of a bridge.

tabouret.etymology: Formed in Middle French as the diminutive of Old French tabour ('cylindrical drum', an older cousin of tambour), because early round low stools were shaped like small drums!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: tabouret (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tabouret

tabouret.notes: At the court of Versailles, being granted **le tabouret**—the right to sit on a folding stool in the Queen's presence—was one of the highest honours in France.

tampon.etymology: Nasalized variant of Middle French tapon ('cloth plug, bung, stopper'), borrowed from Frankish *tappo ('plug, tap, peg'); shifted from a pad of cloth dabbed in ink to an ink stamp or postmark.

history.meaning: plug, wadded pad -> inked stamping pad

cognates.meaning: cognate from Old English tæppa ('cask plug, faucet')

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: tampon (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tampon

tampon.notes: On French mail and official notices, **le cachet / le tampon de la poste faisant foi** ('postmark serving as proof of date') is a classic administrative phrase.

tarte.etymology: From twelfth-century Old French tarte ('flat open pastry'), related to Medieval Latin tarta / torta ('round loaf or twisted pastry'). English tart was borrowed directly from Old French tarte.

cognates.meaning: open pastry pie (borrowed from Old French tarte)

rootFamily.gloss: buttered slice of bread with spread

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: tarte (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tarte

tartine.etymology: Attested from the sixteenth century (Rabelais) as a playful diminutive (-ine) of tarte: a slice of bread spread open-faced with butter, jam, or honey like a little flat tart.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: tartine (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tartine

tasse.etymology: Tasse entered Old French (via Provençal tassa or Italian tazza) from Arabic ṭāsa ('shallow metal drinking bowl'), itself borrowed from Persian tāšt ('cup, basin').
tasse.notes: **Une tasse de thé / de café** = a cup of tea / coffee.

te.etymology: Te continues Latin te, the accusative form of tu, the second-person singular pronoun. The Académie records the French word from the tenth century. Modern te is the unstressed object form alongside subject tu and stressed toi; it is shortened to t' before a vowel or silent h.

temps.etymology: Temps continues Latin tempus, which referred to a division of duration, a season or time. The Académie also connects its weather sense with Latin caeli tempus, the state of the sky. That history helps explain why one French word covers both time and weather.

history.meaning: time, a division of duration, season
state of the sky; behind the weather sense

tenir.etymology: Tenir developed from Popular Latin tenire, a remodelling of Classical Latin tenere, to hold or keep. The Académie records the French verb from the tenth century.

thym.etymology: Refashioned with learned Greek-Latin spelling from Old French tin, borrowed via Classical Latin thymum from Ancient Greek thýmon ('thyme'), connected to thýein ('to burn fragrant offerings, send up sweet smoke').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French tym, likewise given learned th- spelling

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: thym (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: thym

thym.notes: Tied with **persil** and bay leaf (**laurier**) using kitchen **ficelle**, **le thym** forms the classic French **bouquet garni**.

thé.etymology: Borrowed in the seventeenth century via Dutch thee (and Malay teh) from Hokkien Chinese tê ('tea'), brought through maritime trade, whereas land-route varieties of Chinese cha gave Russian čaj and Portuguese chá.
thé.notes: Gives **la théière** ('teapot'). **Du thé au citron / à la menthe** = lemon / mint tea.

théière.etymology: Théière was coined in late seventeenth-century French from thé ('tea') + the vessel suffix -ière (modelled on cafetière 'coffee pot').

tilleul.etymology: Tilleul comes from Popular Latin *tiliolus, diminutive of Classical Latin tilia ('linden or lime tree'), via Old French tilluel. Fragrant linden trees have shaded French courtyards and village squares for centuries.
tilleul.notes: In cafés, **un tilleul** also means a calming evening infusion made from dried linden blossoms.

tisane.etymology: Inherited via Old French tisane from Classical Latin ptisana, borrowed from Ancient Greek ptisánē ('peeled barley, soothing warm barley-water infusion', from ptíssein 'to hull or crush grain'), which broadened from medicinal barley water to any gentle herbal infusion.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: tisane (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tisane

tisane.notes: At the Hôtel du Tilleul, the tree in the courtyard itself provides one of France's favourite evening *tisanes*: **une tisane de tilleul** (linden-blossom tea).

toi.etymology: Toi is the stressed pronoun descending from Latin te ('thee, you' accusative): in stressed position Latin long e diphthongised through ei and oi to modern /twa/.
toi.notes: Used after prepositions (*pour toi*, *avec toi*), in *c'est toi*, and in familiar imperatives (*Assieds-toi*).

toit.etymology: Toit descends regularly from Latin tectum ('roof', originally the past participle of tegere 'to cover', cognate with English 'thatch'): -ct- gave -it and e + i evolved through oi to /wa/.
toit.notes: **Sous les toits** = up under the eaves (attic rooms).

ton.etymology: The possessive ton, with feminine ta, continues Latin tuus, tua and tuum. It is recorded in French from the tenth century. The noun ton for tone has a different Greek and Latin history.

torchon.etymology: Inherited from Old French torchon ('twisted wisp of straw or coarse cloth used for wiping'), derived from torcher ('to wipe, rub clean') < Vulgar Latin *torquare, from Classical Latin torquere ('to twist').

history.meaning: to twist -> to twist straw into a scrubbing wisp

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French torche ('twisted resinous tow'), from the same root!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: torchon (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: torchon

torchon.notes: Hence the classic French saying against mixing unlike things: **Il ne faut pas mélanger les torchons et les serviettes** ('Don't mix kitchen dishcloths with table napkins').

touche.etymology: Deverbal noun from toucher ('to touch, strike lightly', from Spoken Latin *toccare, originally an expressive verb for knocking or striking a bell). By the sixteenth century une touche named each lever key touched by a player's fingers on an organ, harpsichord, and later piano.

history.meaning: to touch, strike -> act of touching

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: touche (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: touche

tourner.etymology: Tourner descends from Latin tornare, to shape on a lathe, related to tornus, a lathe. The French verb is recorded from the tenth century and acquired many senses beyond physical turning.

tournevis.etymology: Transparent verb-noun compound attested from the late seventeenth century: tourne ('turns', from tourner) + vis ('screw', Old French vis 'winding stair, screw thread', from Latin vitis 'climbing vine tendril'). Literally 'screw-turner'.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: tournevis (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tournevis

tout.etymology: Tout continues Latin totus, all or whole. The Académie records it from the ninth century. The forms toute, tous and toutes belong to the same French word family.

train.etymology: Train is a noun built in Old French from traîner ('to drag, draw along', from Popular Latin *traginare). Before railways, un train meant a line of packhorses, carriages, or attendants; in the nineteenth century it naturally named a railway train.
train.notes: **Voyage en train** = train journey; **être en train de** = to be in the middle of doing.

trois.etymology: Trois descends from Latin tres, three. The Académie dates the French form to the tenth century.

trottoir.etymology: Formed in French from trotter ('to trot, walk briskly', borrowed from Old High German troton) + place/instrument suffix -oir; first attested for a raised path for horses, then adopted in 1780s Paris for raised stone pedestrian walkways.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: trottoir (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: trottoir

trottoir.notes: Paris built some of its first stone **trottoirs** along the Rue de l'Odéon in 1781 so pedestrians could step clear of muddy carriage wheels.

trouver.etymology: Trouver is traced to reconstructed Popular Latin *tropare, originally inventing rhetorical turns, tunes or verses. The meaning broadened through invent or discover to find. The French word is recorded from the tenth century.

très.etymology: Très developed from Latin trans, beyond, then through and completely. The Académie dates it to the eleventh century. Its modern intensifying sense continues that strengthening use.

trésor.etymology: Inherited via Old French tresor (with early Gallo-Romance insertion of -r-) from Classical Latin thesaurus ('hoard, treasury'), borrowed from Ancient Greek thēsaurós ('storehouse, treasure chest').

cognates.meaning: treasure came from Old French tresor; thesaurus directly from Greco-Latin

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: trésor (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: trésor

trésor.notes: **Trésor** and English **thesaurus** ('a treasure-house of words') are exact doublets!

tu.etymology: Tu continues Latin tu, the second-person singular pronoun. The Académie dates the French word to the tenth century. Its familiar singular use today continues a very old grammatical distinction between addressing one person and addressing several.

tutoyer.etymology: Tutoyer was built in sixteenth-century French from the pronoun tu ('familiar you') + toi + -er, meaning 'to address someone using tu rather than vous'.
tutoyer.notes: Its polite counterpart is **vouvoyer** ('to address using *vous*'). **On se tutoie?** = Shall we use *tu*?

un.etymology: Un descends from Latin unus, one or a single one. Uses as a number, an indefinite article and a pronoun developed around that source; feminine une belongs to the same series.

utiliser.etymology: Utiliser was formed in French from utile ('useful', from Latin utilis, itself from uti 'to use') + verbal suffix -iser.

valise.etymology: Borrowed in the sixteenth century from Italian valigia ('travelling bag, saddlebag'), a word of debated origin (often linked to Medieval Latin valisia). It replaced older words for leather saddlebags and became the standard French word for a suitcase.
valise.notes: Faire sa valise = to pack one's suitcase; boucler sa valise = to zip/fasten one's bag.

valse.etymology: Borrowed at the end of the eighteenth century from German Walzer ('waltz', literally 'revolving dance'), agent noun from walzen ('to roll, revolve, glide in circles').

cognates.meaning: dance in 3/4 time (also borrowed from German Walzer)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: valse (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: valse

vapeur.etymology: Borrowed in Old French from Classical Latin vapor, vaporem ('steam, warm exhalation, mist').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: vapeur (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: vapeur

vapeur.notes: Like other Latin *-or* abstract nouns (**la chaleur**, **la couleur**, **la douleur**), **la vapeur** became feminine in French, though **un vapeur** (m) meant a steamship!

velours.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French from Old Occitan velos ('shaggy, velvety cloth', altered in northern French to velours by suffix substitution), inherited from Classical Latin villosus ('shaggy, covered with soft nap'), from villus ('tuft of soft hair, nap').

cognates.meaning: velour borrowed from French velours; velvet via Anglo-Norman veluet

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: velours (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: velours

velours.notes: Remember that the final *-s* in **le velours** **/vəluʁ/** is silent, and **faire patte de velours** means 'to draw in one's claws and act with gentle charm'.

venir.etymology: Venir descends from Latin venire, with the same basic meaning to come. The Académie dates the French verb to the ninth century. Its many later constructions still use the idea of something arriving or coming about, including its use as a helper in venir de followed by an infinitive.

vernis.etymology: Inherited from Old French verniz / vernis ('golden resinous finish'), via Medieval Latin vernix / veronix from Medieval Greek beroníkē, named after the Cyrenaican city of Berenice (modern Benghazi), famed in antiquity for exporting fragrant sandarac resin.

history.meaning: city of Berenice -> golden resin exported from there

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French vernis / vernisser

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: vernis (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: vernis

vernis.notes: In the 19th century, painters brushing a final coat of **vernis** onto canvases on the eve of an exhibition gave the world **le vernissage** ('opening-night art reception').

vinaigre.etymology: Transparent Old French compound of vin ('wine', from Latin vinum) + aigre ('sour, sharp, tart', from Latin acrem), literally 'sour wine'.

cognates.meaning: borrowed directly from Old French vinaigre

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: vinaigre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: vinaigre

vinaigre.notes: Because its mild acetic acid dissolves limescale without leaving a film, **le vinaigre blanc** has been a traditional French window-cleaning secret for generations.

vingt.etymology: Vingt continues later Latin vinti, an altered form of viginti, twenty. The Académie records the French word from the eleventh century.

violon.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-16th century from Italian violone / violino (built on viola 'viol', sharing the medieval Provençal and Italian string-instrument family of Old Occitan viola).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: violon (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: violon

violon.notes: Lyon and Mirecourt became major French centers of **la lutherie** from the 16th century onward, crafting **violons** right alongside Italian Cremona.

vitre.etymology: Learned or semi-learned medieval borrowing from Classical Latin vitrum ('glass'), specialised in French to mean a flat windowpane while inherited verre (also from vitrum!) kept the general senses 'glass material' and 'drinking glass'—a classic French etymological doublet.

rootFamily.gloss: glass (popular doublet from the same Latin vitrum)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: vitre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: vitre

voir.etymology: Voir continues Latin videre, to see. The Académie records the French verb from the tenth century.

volet.etymology: Formed on voler ('to fly, swing lightly', from Latin volare) + -et. After naming light fluttering ribbons, cloth sorting trays, and hinged triptych panels, un volet came in the seventeenth century to mean a hinged wooden shutter swinging open and shut across a window.

history.meaning: light cloth; hinged panel of a triptych

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: volet (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: volet

votre.etymology: Votre descends from Popular Latin *voster (Classical Latin vester, 'your', built on vos 'you' by analogy with noster 'our'). As s before t fell silent in French, voster became vostre, modern votre.
votre.notes: Singular **votre** (*votre chambre*), plural **vos** (*vos clés*); stressed pronoun **le vôtre** keeps the circumflex.

vouloir.etymology: Vouloir developed from reconstructed popular Latin *volere, a remodelling of Classical Latin velle, to want. The Académie dates the French verb to the ninth century. The asterisk marks the reconstructed form: it should not be mistaken for an ordinary quoted spelling from a surviving text.

history.meaning: a remodelled infinitive meaning to want

vous.etymology: Vous continues Latin vos, the second-person plural pronoun. The Académie dates it to the tenth century. Modern French uses this plural form both for several addressees and, politely, for one person.
vous.notes:
- Verb agreement is always plural: *vous êtes*, even for one person.
- Participles and adjectives agree with the real referent: *Vous êtes content* (one man), *contente* (one woman).

vraiment.etymology: Vraiment is a French derivative of vrai, true. The Académie records it from the twelfth century; its uses include both truly and the conversational intensifier really.

vérifier.etymology: Vérifier was borrowed from Medieval Latin verificare ('to make true, confirm to be true', from verus 'true' + facere 'to make').
vérifier.notes: Everyday French verb for 'to check' (*vérifier la cave*, *vérifier l'adresse*).

y.etymology: The pronoun y continues Latin hic, here. The Académie records it from the ninth century. It is a different dictionary entry from the name of the letter y.

à.etymology: À principally continues Latin ad, towards or for. Later spoken Latin extended its grammatical uses into relationships now expressed with à in French. The Académie also identifies a separate source a(b) in some expressions, so not every use has one simple origin.

âge.etymology: Âge was formed with the suffix -age from older French aé or ée, continuing Latin aetas, age. The Académie records early forms e(d)age and aage.

ça.etymology: In its everyday pronoun use, ça is a shortened or altered form of cela. The Académie dates that use to the seventeenth century. The psychoanalytic noun has a separate later history.

échelle.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin scala ('ladder, flight of steps', related to scandere 'to climb'). Spoken Latin added a prosthetic vowel before initial sc- (*escala), yielding Old French eschiele, then échelle.

cognates.meaning: graduated measure; to climb (via Latin scala)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: échelle (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: échelle

énigme.etymology: Learned Renaissance borrowing from Classical Latin aenigma, itself from Ancient Greek aínigma ('riddle, dark saying'), derived from ainíssomai ('to speak in hints', from aînos 'meaningful tale').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: énigme (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: énigme

énigme.notes: Watch the gender: although Latin *aenigma* was neuter, **une énigme** settled in modern French as a feminine noun.

éponge.etymology: Inherited via Old French esponge from Latin spongia, borrowed from Ancient Greek spongía ('sea sponge'). Gallo-Romance added a vowel before initial sp- (*ispongia -> esponge -> éponge).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: éponge (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: éponge

éponge.notes: Initial **é-** regularly corresponds to English *s-* before *p, t, c* (**éponge** / *sponge*, **étoile** / *stellar*, **école** / *school*).

équitation.etymology: Équitation is a sixteenth-century borrowing from imperial Latin equitatio, horse riding. Its history is a specific Latin borrowing rather than a generic story inferred from the French ending.

étage.etymology: Étage comes from Old French estage ('dwelling, floor level', from Vulgar Latin *staticum, built on stare 'to stand' — a 'standing level'). English 'stage' was borrowed from Old French estage.
étage.notes: Remember French floor numbering: **le rez-de-chaussée** = ground floor, **le premier étage** = one flight up.

étagère.etymology: Eighteenth-century derivative of étage ('storey, tier, level', from Old French estage 'standing place, level', built on Latin stare 'to stand'): originally an open piece of furniture with stacked tiers of shelves, then any individual shelf.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: étagère (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: étagère

étiquette.etymology: From Middle French estiquette ('small pointed peg or paper slip stuck onto a courtroom sack of legal files'), derived from Old French estiquier ('to stick, pierce'), borrowed from Frankish *stikkan ('to prick, stick fast').

history.meaning: identifying label pinned to a file bag; court protocol card

cognates.meaning: ticket and etiquette both come from French étiquette!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: étiquette (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: étiquette

étiquette.notes: Written slips (**étiquettes**) listing ceremonial rules at royal courts gave Europe the word **etiquette**, while earlier Middle French **estiquet** gave English **ticket**.

étui.etymology: Deverbal noun from Old French estuier ('to enclose safely, treasure, keep with care'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *studiare ('to tend zealously to', from Classical Latin studium 'care, zeal').

history.meaning: to sheathe safely -> protective fitted case

cognates.meaning: learned cousin from the same Latin studium

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: étui (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: étui

étui.notes: Unlike a boxy **boîte**, **un étui** follows the shape of the treasured object inside (**un étui à violon**, **un étui à lunettes**).

être.etymology: Être combines two historical sources. Its main line is Latin esse through reconstructed popular Latin *essere. Forms such as étant, été and étais also continue Old French estere, from Latin stare, meaning to stand or remain.

history.meaning: to stand or remain; from Latin stare

être.notes: Être is highly irregular. It forms compound tenses with reflexive verbs and with verbs such as aller, venir and partir. Many other verbs of movement use avoir, so learn the auxiliary with the verb.

œuf.etymology: Œuf comes from Popular Latin *ovum (Classical Latin ovum, 'egg'). Notice how French pronounces the final f in the singular **un œuf** (/œf/) while dropping it in the plural **des œufs** (/ø/), reflecting Old French sound changes before plural -s.
